Part I — Active Directory (forest, domain, OU).
The identity foundation. The forest is the security boundary; everything else sits inside it.
AD cannot function without DNS, and the AD domain name
a DNS name, so namespace design is shared with Part I.
Kerberos, certificate validity, and log correlation all depend on synchronized time.
Depends on identity (Part I), name resolution (Part II), and time (Part III) before it can issue or validate anything.
Addresses endpoints and, through dynamic update, writes into DNS (Part II); its security leans on the switch layer and on AD authorization.

Each part keeps its own structure: a TL;DR, an authoritative source table, one section per design area, a “where authorities agree, differ, or conflict” section, and its own caveats. This front section adds only the connective tissue — it does not replace any part.

Each part walks the real decisions (e.g., “how many forests,” “AD-integrated vs file-based zones,” “failover vs split-scope”), the realistic options, what each US authority recommends, the trade-offs, and the conflicts — rather than cataloging sources.

Microsoft for the Windows implementation; NIST, CISA/NSA, DISA, and CIS for the security overlay; the IETF (and ICANN for DNS) for the protocols. Clearly-labeled US-company practitioner research (SpecterOps, Trimarc, Mandiant, Akamai) is included as non-governmental.

Some parts were produced with full Research; others (where Research was unavailable in-session) were built from direct source checks plus the project’s earlier research and are flagged accordingly in their own caveats. Part III (NTP) is a prerequisite for Part I’s Kerberos 5- minute skew tolerance, for Part IV’s certificate

and CRL validity windows, and for the log-correlation requirement (NIST AU-8 / SC-45) that recurs in every part. The forest-root PDC emulator is the single external time boundary and also a Part I FSMO role — so a PDC-emulator move touches both references.
The forest is the blast radius.
, not the domain, is the security boundary. That is exactly what Part IV’s “treat every CA as Tier 0,” Part IV’s
NTAuth/strong-mapping enforcement, and Part I’s own administrative-tier model all exist to protect. Compromise of Tier 0 anywhere is forest-wide.
Namespace is one decision shared by two parts.
The AD domain name (Part I) and the DNS zone name (Part II) are the same string: use a registered subdomain or ICANN’s
. Read Part I §2 and Part II §1 together.

Part V’s DHCP–DNS dynamic-update design (the DnsUpdateProxy problem, Name Protection/DHCID, the dedicated registration credential) is the same seam as Part II’s dynamic-update and scavenging design. The Akamai DDSpoof and “DHCP Administrators → Domain Admins” findings live at this seam and tie Part V back to Parts I and II.

Part IV’s domain-controller certificates (Kerberos Authentication template), strong certificate mapping (KB5014754), and NTAuth chaining (KB5057784) are the mechanism behind Part I’s certificate-based authentication — and both now depend on Microsoft’s enforcement, which removed the registry bypasses in 2025.

. For those two, the IETF defines the protocol, Microsoft defines the Windows behavior, DISA supplies one hard rule each (DHCP log retention; the forest-root external-time requirement), and the security load shifts to the switch layer (DHCP) or to a non- Microsoft layer (authenticated NTP).

overview.text: Cross-cutting agreements and conflicts (across all five)

spans.t: Where the US authorities consistently agree:
The forest is the security boundary; isolate and tier the identity control plane (Tier 0).
Prefer the fewest moving parts that meet the requirement (single forest, single domain, dedicated-but-minimal servers).
Synchronized time is mandatory, and logs must carry UTC timestamps for correlation.
Centralize and retain security-relevant logs; forward them off-box.
The conflicts that recur across parts:
Dedicated servers vs co-location with domain controllers.

NIST prefers dedicated DNS (Part II) and keeping roles off DCs (recurs for DHCP in Part V and CAs in Part IV); Microsoft’s model co-locates DNS on DCs and historically co- located DHCP on DCs. The defensible middle ground differs per service and is stated in each part.
DISA hard rules vs Microsoft defaults.

DISA mandates things Microsoft leaves optional or ships off by default — internal-zone DNSSEC with NSEC3 (Part II), the external DoD time source (Part III), CA-manager approval for SAN-suppliable templates (Part IV), and 30- day-online/1-year-offline DHCP log retention (Part V). DoD systems follow DISA; others treat these as benchmarks.

The IETF, NSA, and CISA call for authenticated time (Part III), but the Windows Time Service cannot authenticate to any external NTP server — so this has to be solved on routers, appliances, or a non-Windows time layer. This gap quietly affects the integrity of everything time-dependent above.

NIST and NSA set deprecation dates for SHA-1 (by 2030) and quantum- vulnerable RSA/ECDSA (draft: after 2030/2035), and AD CS on Windows Server 2025 can now issue ML-DSA certificates (Part IV) — but existing CAs can’t be converted, so this is a parallel- hierarchy pilot, not a migration.
This is review material, not published guidance.
It is here for the owner’s review before anything is used in the training library, website, or app.

Each part’s own “Caveats” section is authoritative for what was and wasn’t confirmed in that part. Common threads: DISA STIG release numbers were often read from third-party mirrors rather than cyber.mil; some CIS benchmark versions and draft-NIST dates were not re-verified; a few Microsoft default values come from documentation not re-fetched for that edition.

Everything is stated as of October 2026. Protocol and product facts (RFC 9915 replacing RFC 8415, Windows Server 2025 functional level and ML-DSA, strong- mapping/NTAuth enforcement, the October 2026 CGPM leap-second decision) are current to that date and should be re-checked over time.

spans.t: US guidance on Active Directory design splits cleanly. Microsoft owns the structural logic (how many forests and domains, how to lay out OUs and Group Policy); CISA/NSA, DISA and NIST own the security overlay (tiered administration, privileged-access isolation, and the controls that keep a forest from falling in one move). The single fact they all agree on is that
the forest, not the domain, is the security boundary

, so forest and tiering decisions set the blast radius for an identity compromise. The two points of real movement in 2026 are the retirement of the old “Red Forest” (ESAE) design in favor of the Enterprise Access Model, and Windows Server 2025’s delegated Managed Service Accounts, which created a new Tier 0 concern (BadSuccessor / CVE-2025-53779).
This reference parallels the companion DNS, PKI, NTP and DHCP design references: organized by design area, US sources only, ending with where the authorities agree, differ, or conflict.

Microsoft, NIST, CISA/NSA, DISA, CIS, and (minimally) the IETF for the underlying Kerberos and LDAP protocols. US-company practitioner research (SpecterOps, Trimarc, Mandiant, Akamai) is included and labeled as non-governmental.
non-US government guidance — ANSSI (France), BSI (Germany), NCSC (UK), ASD/ACSC (Australia), CCCS (Canada), ENISA (EU).
forest, domain, and OU, plus the design areas tied to them — trusts, Group Policy, and administrative tiering.

Prefer a single production forest unless a hard isolation or autonomy requirement forces more. Microsoft states the forest is “the security and administrative boundary for all objects that reside within the forest,” and that co-ownership of one forest by two autonomous IT organizations “is not recommended.” A separate administrative (“Red”) forest is no longer the default — ESAE was retired on December 15, 2020 and replaced by the Enterprise Access Model — but tiering itself was not retired.
Prefer a single domain per forest. The domain is a replication and administrative boundary,

a security boundary. Add domains only for replication, administrative, or policy reasons, never for security isolation. The AD domain name is a DNS name, so namespace choice is a joint AD/DNS decision (use a registered subdomain or ICANN’s
Design OUs for exactly two purposes — delegation of administration and Group Policy application — not replication. Delegate with least privilege, redirect the default
containers so GPOs reach new objects, and build a Tier 0/1/2 OU structure for administrative separation.

Keep GPOs few and well-scoped. Understand LSDOU processing, link order, Block Inheritance vs Enforced, security and WMI filtering, and loopback. Deliver security baselines (DISA STIG GPOs, Microsoft security baselines, CIS build kits) through GPOs linked to the right OUs, tested first.

Treat the directory’s control plane as Tier 0 (domain controllers, AD CS, AD FS, Microsoft Entra Connect, and the accounts, groups and workstations that manage them). Use privileged access workstations and the clean- source principle, put privileged accounts in Protected Users with authentication policies/silos, set
to 0, and restrict OU write permissions so the dMSA/BadSuccessor path is closed.

spans.t: how many forests to run, how to treat the forest security boundary, how to build the forest root domain, which forest functional level to choose, and whether a separate administrative forest is warranted.

single forest with a single domain (simplest, most common); single forest with multiple domains (one security boundary, several administrative/replication boundaries); multiple forests (account/resource or organizational forests for isolation/autonomy); a dedicated administrative forest (the former ESAE/“Red Forest”, now niche).

“A forest is the security and administrative boundary for all objects that reside within the forest. In contrast, a domain is the administrative boundary for managing objects.” The domain was the security boundary in the Windows NT era; that changed with Active Directory.

Determining the number of forests means evaluating isolation and autonomy requirements; “isolation requirements limit your design choices,” and the decision “involves balancing costs against benefits.”
All objects in one forest are in the global catalog, so “no synchronization across forests is required.” Co-ownership of a single forest by two autonomous IT organizations “is not recommended.”
Collapsing forests later is much harder than adding them, so get the count right at the start.

Windows Server 2025 introduces a new domain and forest functional level (the first since 2016); a new forest requires at least the 2016 level. The 2025 level enables the optional 32k database page size and the delegated Managed Service Account (dMSA) feature.
either a dedicated/empty root (holding the forest-wide Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins groups, isolating them) or a single regional domain that is also the root.

ESAE (the “Red Forest”) was retired as the default recommendation on December 15, 2020, when Microsoft published the Enterprise Access Model. SpecterOps confirms Microsoft “retired ESAE and took down their old recommendations,” and that the equivalent control is now the Enterprise Access Model plus the administrative tier model.

A dedicated administrative forest (and Microsoft’s PAM/MIM pattern) still exists for the highest-assurance or legacy on-prem cases, but most organizations should implement tiering and PAWs within the production forest rather than stand up a separate forest.

treat the forest as the identity control plane’s outer edge. The Sept 2024 CISA/NSA guidance frames AD compromise as the primary objective for attackers; because the forest is the security boundary, Tier 0 isolation (Section 6) is what limits damage. NIST SP 800-207 reframes identity as the control plane, the conceptual basis for isolating it.

forest-level rules live in the AD Forest STIG — SID filtering and selective authentication on trusts (Section 3), restrictions on anonymous access to forest data, and the AD CS rules (V-269098/V-269099).

give real isolation (separate schemas and security boundaries; a compromise in one does not automatically cross), at the cost of synchronization (no shared global catalog; you need Entra Connect / MIM / trusts), duplicated administration, and a worse cross-forest user experience.
is cheaper and simpler but concentrates risk: a Tier 0 compromise anywhere in the forest is a whole-forest compromise.
maximizes credential isolation but is expensive and complex; Microsoft retired it as the default for that reason.

the main one is “when is a separate administrative forest still justified?” Microsoft now answers “rarely — use the Enterprise Access Model in-forest,” while practitioners note the tier model persists and a hardened admin forest remains defensible for specific high-assurance or heavily legacy estates. There is no US-government mandate for a separate admin forest.
how many domains per forest, how to treat the domain boundary, single vs multiple trees/namespaces, whether to use an empty forest-root domain, the domain functional level, and FSMO placement.
single domain (preferred); multiple domains in one tree (contiguous namespace); multiple trees (disjoint namespaces) in one forest; an empty forest-root domain plus one or more child domains.
The domain is “the administrative boundary for managing objects,” not a security boundary. “Only one instance of an Active Directory domain should exist at any time.”

Microsoft’s long-standing guidance favors the fewest domains possible, and a single domain wherever it meets requirements. Extra domains are justified by replication control, decentralized administration, distinct account/password or policy requirements, or replication scale —
by a desire for security isolation, because domain admins in one domain can reach others through known forest-internal paths.

a dedicated root domain that holds the forest-wide groups (Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins) and little else, to protect those groups and decouple the root from any region. It adds domain controllers to build and maintain.
governs per-domain features; raising it requires all domain controllers at that OS level or higher.

five operations master roles — Schema Master and Domain Naming Master are forest-wide; PDC Emulator, RID Master, and Infrastructure Master are per-domain. Place the PDC Emulator on a reliable, well-connected DC (it is also the default authoritative time source — see the NTP reference); keep the Infrastructure Master off a global catalog server unless every DC is a GC. Seize a role only after unrecoverable failure.
Kerberos (RFC 4120) and LDAP (RFC 4511) are the protocols the domain exposes; design choices (trust transitivity, referrals) rest on them.
simplest administration, one Group Policy and replication scope, easiest recovery. It offers no internal administrative separation beyond OUs and delegation.
security isolation, plus more DCs, trusts to manage, and cross-domain Group Policy complexity.
protects forest-wide groups and gives a stable root, at the cost of extra infrastructure; modern guidance leans toward single-domain for most organizations.

single vs multiple domains, and whether an empty root is worth it. Microsoft historically recommended an empty root for large enterprises; current practice leans single- domain. No US authority treats a domain as a security boundary — a common and dangerous misconception the sources explicitly correct.
which trust relationships to create, their direction and transitivity, and how to contain the risk they add.
— created automatically between all domains in a forest; two-way and transitive; Kerberos.
— to a single domain in another forest; non-transitive.
— between two forest root domains; transitive across each forest.
— to a non-Windows Kerberos realm (e.g., MIT Kerberos).
— to optimize authentication paths within a large forest.

can be set on external/forest trusts so that only explicitly allowed users can authenticate to specific resources across the trust.

A forest trust is a convenience, not a security guarantee: a compromise in a trusted forest can threaten the trusting forest, so a forest trust should not be treated as a security boundary against a compromised partner.
SID filtering must be enabled on inter-forest/external trusts, and selective authentication applied where cross-forest access must be limited.

the Sept 2024 guidance covers trust-account abuse, SID-history injection, and cross-forest Kerberoasting among its techniques; the practical message is that trusts widen the attack surface and must be minimized and filtered.

trusts enable resource and identity sharing across boundaries, but every trust enlarges the reachable attack surface. SID filtering can break legacy migrations that rely on SID history; selective authentication adds per-resource management overhead.

default SID filtering vs migration needs (filtering must sometimes be relaxed temporarily, which is risky). And the framing of a forest trust: Microsoft and CISA/NSA are clear it is not a security boundary against a compromised trusted forest, even though it is often treated as one in practice.
how to structure organizational units, how to delegate administration, where to place objects, and how to ensure Group Policy reaches everything.

a replication or security boundary (that is domains/forests and sites).
— top-level OUs for Users, Computers, Groups, Service Accounts.
— e.g., Servers, Workstations, by business function.
— regional OUs for delegated regional admins.

Build the OU design to delegate administration and to apply Group Policy; structure follows those two needs rather than the org chart.
Delegate with the Delegation of Control Wizard or custom ACLs, granting the minimum rights needed and documenting them; review delegated permissions over time.

Protect OUs from accidental deletion, and avoid unnecessarily deep nesting (it complicates both delegation and Group Policy processing).

Too many OUs or deep nesting slows and obscures Group Policy processing and makes delegation hard to audit.
Container redirection is a one-time action but essential; skipping it leaves default-created accounts outside GPO scope.
OU-by-function vs OU-by-geography — both valid, and the right choice depends on who delegates administration and what policy varies. And whether to use Block Inheritance on an OU (see Section 5).

Tier 0 systems get the strictest baselines, scoped by the tiering OUs.

fewer, well-named, well-scoped GPOs mean faster logon/boot and far easier troubleshooting. Block Inheritance and heavy security/WMI filtering make the effective-policy picture hard to reason about; over-blocking is a common cause of baseline drift.
Block Inheritance (discouraged — it hides policy) vs Enforced (use sparingly for must-apply security settings); and security-group filtering vs OU-based targeting as the primary scoping method.

how to isolate privileged access — the tier model and the Enterprise Access Model, what belongs in Tier 0, how to use privileged access workstations and the clean-source principle, and how to protect privileged accounts and the newest attack primitives.

The AD DS tier model “separates administrative identities, workstations, and managed assets into trust tiers” — Tier 0, Tier 1, Tier 2 — with privileged access workstations (PAWs) enforcing the boundaries.
contains everything that directly or indirectly controls the directory: domain controllers; identity services including
Microsoft Entra Connect, Microsoft Entra application proxy, AD FS, and AD CS
; and Tier 0 administrative accounts and groups, “including built-in Active Directory groups such as Backup Operators and Server Operators.”
The tier model fits inside the broader
(EAM), which spans on- premises, multiple clouds, user access, and application access via a control plane, management plane, and data/workload plane. The model and deployment guidance are in the
administer a tier only from a device of equal or higher trust (manage Tier 0 only from a Tier 0 PAW).
security group hardens privileged accounts (no NTLM, no DES/RC4, no unconstrained delegation, no long-term Kerberos keys, no credential caching).
restrict where privileged accounts can authenticate.
Microsoft retired ESAE/the Red Forest on December 15, 2020 and replaced it with the Enterprise Access Model; the
tier model itself was not retired

AC-2 (account management), AC-5 (separation of duties), AC-6 least privilege with AC-6(2) (non-privileged access for nonsecurity functions) and AC-6(5) (privileged accounts restricted to named personnel), and IA-2(1) (MFA for privileged accounts). SP 800-63B(-4) sets authenticator assurance; SP 800-207 establishes identity as the control plane.

Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, DCSync, Golden/Silver Ticket, AD CS abuse, unconstrained delegation, SID-history injection, GPO abuse, and more. Mitigations include tiering, PAWs, Protected Users, MFA, least privilege, and setting the machine-account quota to zero. It treats AD CS, AD FS and Entra Connect as Tier 0.

CAT I rules restrict membership of Enterprise Admins, Domain Admins and Schema Admins (Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins are typically kept empty except when a specific change requires them); V-243477 requires privileged domain accounts to be in the Protected Users group; and AD remote management must come from a PAW/Tier 0.
Controls v8.1 Safeguard 5.4 (dedicated administrative accounts) and the MFA safeguards; the Windows Server benchmarks harden the hosts.
the default of 10 lets any authenticated user join 10 computers (machine accounts), which enables several escalation primitives; the common hardening is to set it to 0.

Windows Server 2025 introduced delegated Managed Service Accounts to migrate legacy service accounts. The BadSuccessor technique (Akamai, Yuval Gordon; disclosed May 21, 2025; patched August 12, 2025) abuses them: in any forest with at least one Windows Server 2025 domain controller and a KDS root key, an attacker who can create a dMSA — or who merely has write permission to any OU, plus the ability to set the dMSA’s migration attributes (e.g.,
) — can impersonate a privileged account and reach domain, then forest, compromise. Notably the domain does
need to be at the 2025 functional level or using dMSAs. Design implications: apply the patch to all Windows Server 2025 DCs, restrict OU write permissions, and ensure
only Tier 0 can create or manage dMSAs and their migration attributes
. Akamai notes the patch mitigates much of the risk but the technique “lives on” in some scenarios.

strict tiering is the single highest-value AD security control, but it is operationally heavy — dedicated accounts per tier, PAWs, and discipline about never signing a Tier 0 credential into a lower-tier host. The cost is hardware and process; the payoff is that a workstation or server compromise no longer yields the directory.
DISA’s CAT I rules target Enterprise Admins / Domain Admins / Schema Admins specifically, while Microsoft’s tier model protects
Tier 0 groups (including Backup Operators, Server Operators, AD CS, AD FS, Entra Connect). DISA compliance alone therefore does not equal full tier isolation.
Microsoft’s current guidance pushes cloud-era tooling (the Enterprise Access Model, Microsoft Defender for Identity, Entra PIM), while DISA and NIST remain platform-neutral and on-prem-centric.
as of this writing, no US-government source addresses dMSA/BadSuccessor directly; the Tier 0 guidance for dMSAs comes from Microsoft’s CVE response and practitioners (SpecterOps, Akamai, Tenable).

spans.t: The US guidance baseline treats Active Directory administration the same way across all authorities checked: Microsoft’s current tier model, Microsoft’s tooling, DISA STIGs, CIS, and the CISA/NSA joint guidance all require separating privileged identities by tier. That means dedicated admin accounts, privileged access workstations (PAWs), and rules that block higher- tier credentials from lower-tier systems. Only the separate “Red Forest” (ESAE) admin-forest architecture was retired, in December 2020. Tiering itself was not. NIST supplies the control language (AC-2, AC-5, AC-6(5), IA-2) without naming AD. DISA turns the model into mandatory, auditable rules. IETF RFCs supply only protocol background.

blocks.text: 5. Where authorities agree, differ, or conflict

spans.t: Microsoft retired the separate admin forest, not the tier concept. Its 2026 tier-model page and the GitHub framework expand tiering. DISA (PAW STIG “administrative tier,” V-269099 “PAW tier 0”) and CISA/NSA still use tier language. Training content should not present “Red Forest” as current Microsoft guidance, nor present tiering as deprecated.
NIST maps onto the tier model without naming it.
AC-5 corresponds to Microsoft’s “operators, approvers, auditors.”
AC-6(2) and AC-6(5) correspond to dedicated, tier-scoped admin accounts.
IA-2(1) corresponds to MFA for admins.
NIST is outcome-based; Microsoft and DISA supply the AD mechanisms.
DISA is prescriptive; Microsoft provides a framework.
DISA fixes group names (EA/DA) in Deny rights and requires Protected Users membership. These are binary, auditable checks.
Microsoft frames tiers by control scope and accepts organizational variation, such as Tier 0 membership beyond DA and the “common target” of fewer than five admins.
DISA’s Deny rights target EA/DA specifically. Microsoft’s model applies to any Tier 0 or Tier 1 group, so DISA compliance alone does not achieve full tier isolation.

Microsoft explicitly includes backup, monitoring, patching, hypervisor, and EDR systems that manage Tier 0. DISA codifies only parts (AD CS via PAW). CISA/NSA emphasize AD CS, AD FS, and Entra Connect. These positions are compatible, but Microsoft’s is the broadest.

Microsoft’s ESAE rationale and EAM push toward cloud-based controls (MDI, PIM, cloud PAWs). DISA and NIST are platform-neutral; DoD environments may be disconnected, which is one of Microsoft’s own ESAE exception cases.

spans.t: US authorities agree on a common DNS baseline for Active Directory, and they disagree in a few specific places. The baseline: name the forest under a domain you have registered. Use AD- integrated zones that accept only secure dynamic updates. Run DNS as at least two fault- tolerant servers that keep internal and external roles apart. Send all outbound resolution through an authorized, policy-enforcing (Protective DNS) forwarder, and block every other path to the internet. Turn off LLMNR, NetBIOS name resolution and mDNS. Log DNS centrally on synchronized time. The authorities disagree on DNSSEC for internal zones, on NSEC versus NSEC3, on whether DNS should run on domain controllers or on dedicated servers, and on how to build split-brain DNS. NIST SP 800-81r3 (March 2026) and the DISA Windows DNS STIG are the two US documents that most often pull in opposite directions.
Name the forest as a subdomain of a domain you have registered, or use ICANN’s reserved

or single-label names. Store zones in AD with “Secure only” updates. Run at least two DNS servers on different network segments. Resolvers should forward only to an approved Protective DNS service, outbound port-53, DoT and DoH should be blocked for everything else, and recursion should be off on any authoritative server that faces the internet. Disable LLMNR, NetBIOS and mDNS. Send DNS analytic and audit logs to a SIEM on synchronized time.
NIST SP 800-81r3 recommends DNSSEC for zones that face the internet. It advises

signing internal zones unless a policy requires it, and it prefers NSEC to NSEC3. The DISA STIG requires DNSSEC records, NSEC3 for all internal zones, and client validation enforced through the NRPT. Signing with SHA-1 is now prohibited (RFC 9905, November 2025); use ECDSA P-256/P-384 or RSA/SHA-256 with keys of 2048 bits or more. Windows Server 2025 DNS has supported client-facing DoH since the June 2026 security update, but traffic to forwarders, zone transfers and dynamic updates is still unencrypted.

NIST says DNS should run on dedicated servers, while Microsoft’s AD-integrated design puts DNS on domain controllers. DISA wants split DNS on separate internal and external servers, while Microsoft supports split-brain through DNS policies on a single server. Root-hint fallback conflicts with the federal rule that all outbound DNS goes through Protective DNS. Read each control in light of the authority that applies to you: FCEB (CISA/OMB), DoD (DISA), or general enterprise (Microsoft/NIST/CIS).

Use DNS names registered with an internet authority, and do not use single-label DNS names.
If the organization has an internet presence, use names relative to the registered name. The example given is
Avoid “names that are used in internet-standard special features, such as .local,” and avoid top-level internet names on an intranet because of resolution errors.
Since Windows Server 2008 R2, Dcpromo has not allowed single-label domain names.

For DNSSEC and mobile hosts it notes that “network administrators can avoid this problem by using different names for internal and external zones”. If internal zones are signed, it recommends a separate delegation from the external parent so a chain of trust exists, while acknowledging that this leaks the delegation name.

keeps user principal names and URLs identical inside and out. The cost is maintaining two copies of the same zone. Public records must be mirrored internally, or internal clients cannot reach the public site.
A subdomain of a registered name

is unambiguous, can get publicly trusted certificates, and gives a clean chain of trust for DNSSEC. Its weakness is that internal names may leak in queries to public resolvers unless outbound DNS is controlled.

One forest with one contiguous tree is simplest.
Several trees, or forests linked by trust, need conditional forwarders or stub/secondary zones (see §2–3).
Microsoft notes that DCs cannot forward-resolve the other forest’s names if those names are not registered.
None of the US authorities endorse

as an alternative that never collides. These two do not contradict each other, but Microsoft’s AD naming pages do not yet mention

How zones are stored and replicated, who can write to them, and how other namespaces are reached.
AD-integrated primary zones. Replication scope can be:
all DNS servers on DCs in the forest (ForestDnsZones),
all DNS servers on DCs in the domain (DomainDnsZones, the default),
all DCs in the domain (the legacy Windows 2000-compatible domain partition), or
Stub zones, conditional forwarders, or secondary zones
AD-integrated zones replicate through AD rather than zone transfer. Secure dynamic update is supported
for AD-integrated zones and is their default.
Use forest scope when names must be resolvable across domains, for example the
Reverse zones can be created AD-integrated by network ID (for example
For trusts, the remote domain’s DNS records must be resolvable, through forwarders or secondary/stub zones.

GlobalNames holds static CNAMEs for important servers. Dynamic updates cannot register names in it. Support must be enabled on each DNS server. Microsoft describes it as “not designed to be a complete replacement for WINS”.
Secondary servers must cryptographically authenticate zone transfers. The STIG states that for AD-integrated zones this authenticity “is accomplished by AD replication”.
Primaries must send transfers only to listed secondaries.
NS records must point to active authoritative servers.
All authoritative servers must hold the same zone version.
Zone records must be validated annually.
No zone may contain IPv6 link-local addresses, and AAAA records are only for hosts that are actually dual-stack.
Restrict zone transfers with ACLs and authenticate them with TSIG (or SIG(0)). ZONEMD can verify zone integrity, and TLS (XoT) adds confidentiality.
Disable transfers on secondaries unless they feed other secondaries.
Tune SOA refresh between roughly 1200 s and 86400 s to avoid “zone drift/thrash”.
RFC 2317 (BCP 20) defines classless in-addr.arpa delegation using CNAMEs for subnets smaller than /24.
RFC 6303 (BCP 163) says resolvers should serve locally the reverse zones for private and special address space (for example RFC 1918 ranges), so those queries do not leak to the public DNS.
RFC 1912 lists classic configuration errors, such as missing PTRs and CNAMEs at the zone apex.

zones are multi-master and their replication is secured by AD. This satisfies DISA’s authenticated-transfer rule without TSIG. The catch is that the zone can only live on DCs, which ties DNS availability to DC availability (§6).

The Windows DNS server’s support for standard RFC 8945 TSIG on zone transfers was not verifified in this research.
Windows uses GSS-TSIG for secure dynamic update.

NIST frames zone protection in terms of TSIG and ACLs, while Microsoft relies on AD replication. DISA explicitly accepts AD replication as equivalent, so the guidance is consistent in practice.
How internal resolvers reach internal partner namespaces and the internet, and which servers are allowed to recurse.
root hints, forwarders (including a Protective DNS service), or forwarders with root-hint fallback.

On a DC that runs DNS, list a replication partner first and the loopback (127.0.0.1 / ::1) second or third, never first.
The BPA warns that if loopback is first, “Active Directory might be unable to find its replication partners”, and that a DC pointing only to itself can become an “island”.
The first DC in a new forest points to itself.
Never point DCs at an ISP’s DNS servers.
Some Microsoft Q&A answers argue the opposite (self first). The BPA rule is the authoritative published position.
An instance that the internet can reach should be authoritative
Purely internal servers may combine the two roles, which it calls “acceptable and practical”.
Recursive servers should accept queries only from internal clients.
Prohibit recursion on authoritative servers that have no forwarders configured.
Restrict caching servers to known client ranges.
Forwarders on an authoritative Windows DNS server must point only to an internal, non-AD-integrated DNS server or to DoD Enterprise Recursive Services.
Servers authoritative for local zones must point root hints only at the internal root.
requires the name-resolution service to be fault-tolerant and to implement internal/external role separation.
It prefers a hybrid of cloud and on-premises RPZ/DNS firewall where feasible, so that a cloud outage that fails open still leaves local protection.
Block outbound DNS (UDP/TCP 53) from everything except authorized forwarders. Block unauthorized DoT (TCP 853), DoQ (UDP 853) and DoH (RPZ plus firewall).
Use MDM/EMM so users cannot configure unapproved resolvers.

It sets selection criteria such as blocking malware and phishing domains, high availability, logging, and handling of roaming clients.
It warns that the provider can see all your queries, so you must understand how it uses the data.
It explicitly does not endorse any vendor.

Windows Server 2025 DNS gained DoH for client-facing traffic in the February 10, 2026 update (preview). It became generally available with the 2026-06 security update KB5094125.

Microsoft states that upstream traffic (forwarders, conditional forwarders, authoritative servers), zone transfers and dynamic updates “remain unencrypted”. Policies that filter on transport protocol do not match DoH queries.

Microsoft Learn’s “Secure DNS Client over HTTPS (DoH)” page says not to enable “Require DoH” on domain-joined computers, because AD DS relies heavily on DNS and the Windows DNS Server service did not support DoH queries; it suggests IPsec connection security rules for encrypting AD DNS traffic instead. That page predates the 2026 server-side DoH feature.
supports split-brain on a single server through zone scopes and query-resolution policies, including in AD. The zone scopes replicate through AD, but the
and must be copied to each server.
requires internal and external records to be kept separate. With separate servers, the internal server must be unreachable from outside and the external server unreachable from inside resolvers.
No US source recommends root hints in closed networks.
DISA’s internal-root rule and NIST’s egress blocking both point to: no direct external resolution, with an internal root or forwarder hierarchy instead.
ICANN/IANA publish the root hints for internet-connected resolvers.

centralizes policy and logging, but it becomes a single dependency. Fail-open designs reintroduce bypass, which is why NIST suggests on- premises backup protection.

See the conflicts section below: root-hint fallback versus PDNS mandates; whether internal DoH is required or optional; and split-brain on separate servers versus DNS policy.
Who is allowed to create and change records, how stale records are removed, and how DHCP registrations are secured.
client self-registration, or DHCP registering on the client’s behalf.
aging and scavenging on or off.
Secure dynamic update is available only for AD- integrated zones and is the default after conversion. Standard primary zones accept unsecured updates.
A DHCP server that registers on a client’s behalf becomes the

To avoid ownership and stale-record problems, configure DHCP with a dedicated, low-privilege credential for DNS updates and use the DnsUpdateProxy group carefully. Records created by members of DnsUpdateProxy are not secured.
DHCP Name Protection (which uses DHCID records) stops non-Windows clients from taking over names already registered.

Aging and scavenging are disabled by default. The no-refresh and refresh intervals are 7 days each, and the default scavenging period is 7 days. Both server-level scavenging and zone-level aging must be enabled.
Accept updates only from authorized senders (TSIG or ACL); TSIG timestamps help against replay.
Use dedicated hidden primaries for zones that accept dynamic updates, because floods of updates can starve query service.
Keep a history of DHCP leases for incident response.
Restrict dynamic updates to known clients and protect their authenticity through transaction signing.
Record who added, modified or deleted zone data.
The DNS server’s own IP address must be static.

for DCs, DNS servers and other infrastructure avoid accidental scavenging and spoofed registration, but they have to be maintained by hand. Note that DCs register their own SRV records dynamically, and that must keep working.

cuts stale records, which are a source of spoofing and dangling records. Set too short relative to DHCP lease length, it deletes live records. A common rule of thumb is no- refresh plus refresh greater than or equal to the DHCP lease; that rule is not stated in the sources reviewed here.
NIST’s hidden-primary model does not fit AD’s multi-master model, where every DC hosting the zone is a writable primary.
DISA’s “transaction signing” is satisfied by Windows GSS-TSIG secure updates.
Whether to sign zones (external and/or internal), with which algorithm and denial-of-existence method, where the private keys are kept, and whether resolvers and clients validate.
Sign external zones only, sign both external and internal, or sign nothing.
Online signing (keys on the server, which allows dynamic updates) or offline signing.
A KSK/ZSK split or a combined signing key.
RSA/SHA-256 or ECDSA P-256/P- 384 (Ed25519/Ed448 are listed by NIST).
Validation on the resolver only, or with clients enforcing it through the NRPT.
Signing internal zones “is not recommended” unless something (for example, a government requirement) mandates it. The reasons:
It is hard to build a chain of trust without extra trust anchors.
Dynamically updated zones must be re-signed constantly.
It is pointless when the same servers are both authoritative and recursive, which is the usual AD pattern.
Algorithms (Table 1, from RFC 8624, SP 800-57 and SP 800-131A):
ECDSA and EdDSA are preferred because their responses are smaller.
112-bit security strength is acceptable until 2030, after which 128-bit is required.
Keys have a maximum lifetime of 1–3 years.
Store the KSK in an HSM where practical.
Keep DNSKEY RRSIG validity short (about 5–7 days).
Avoid TTLs of 30 s or less on signed data.
Prefer NSEC. If NSEC3 is used, set its parameters per RFC 9276.
Signers and validators need authenticated time (for example NTS).
Validating resolvers should configure the root trust anchor and enable automated RFC 5011 rollover.
Enable DNSSEC records, and validate the authentication chain.
Use NSEC3 for all internal zones, changing the salt at every full re-sign.
The signature algorithm must be FIPS- compatible.
RRSIG validity on DNSKEY and DS should be between 2 days and 1 week.
Keep the ZSK private key only on a server that supports dynamic updates.
If the primary does not take dynamic updates, keep both the KSK and ZSK private keys off it (offline signing).
Export trust anchors and distribute them to validating servers, and enable automatic trust-anchor update.
Use Group Policy NRPT to make clients require DNSSEC validation.
SC-20 requires authoritative responses to carry origin-authentication and integrity artifacts and a verifiable parent–child chain. SC-20(1) has been withdrawn and folded into SC-20.
SC-21 requires resolvers to request and perform that verification.
RFC 6781 covers operational practice: KSK/ZSK roles, rollovers, and algorithm rollover ordering.
RFC 9905 (November 2025) makes RSASHA1 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 “MUST NOT” for signing and SHA-1 DS digests “MUST NOT”. Validators should still accept them during the transition.
RFC 9904 moves algorithm recommendations to the IANA registry.
Windows’ online signing of AD-integrated zones keeps dynamic updates working, but the signing keys stay on DCs. That runs against NIST’s HSM preference and DISA’s offline- key rules for static zones.
NSEC3 slows zone walking. NIST points out that it can often still be reversed and adds CPU cost.
ECDSA keeps responses below fragmentation limits. RSA has wider legacy support.
Note that NSEC3 itself hashes with SHA-1. RFC 9905 deprecates SHA-1
algorithms, not the NSEC3 hash, and NIST says to migrate once a replacement is specified.
Internal signing: NIST says generally don’t; DISA says do.

On algorithms, DISA’s “FIPS-compatible” requirement overlaps with NIST’s table: RSA/SHA-256 and ECDSA are both FIPS 186 algorithms. Microsoft Learn’s “Sign DNS Zones with DNSSEC” page lists RSA/SHA-256 (default), ECDSA P-256/SHA-256, ECDSA P-384/SHA-384, RSA/SHA-512 and the SHA-1 variants, but not Ed25519 or Ed448; its default DS generation includes SHA-1, which RFC 9905 now prohibits.
Whether DNS runs on DCs or on dedicated servers, and how many DNS servers to deploy and where.
AD-integrated DNS on every DC, or on some DCs.
Dedicated (appliance or Windows) resolvers in front of DCs.
“Deploy dedicated DNS servers to reduce attack surfaces”. If that is not feasible, co-locating with related core services such as DHCP may be acceptable.
Every zone needs a primary and one or more secondaries. At least two authoritative servers should sit on different network segments and in different places.
Stubs should be configured with at least two recursive servers. Anycast can hide the loss of a single server, which matters for applications that use only one server.
Remove DNS server software from hosts that are not name servers.
at least two authoritative servers in two geographically separated subnetworks.
Authoritative servers must be geographically dispersed and on different network segments.
There must be a documented procedure to re-role a secondary as primary.
Administrators must be notified when a component fails.
Run DNS on DCs with AD-integrated zones so the DC locator works and replication is secured.
Point member servers and clients only at internal DNS servers.
assets use enterprise-controlled or reputable DNS servers.

simpler, gives multi-master AD-secured replication, and keeps locator records local. On the other hand, a compromise of DNS or a DC affects both services, and DCs then process untrusted recursive traffic.

(forwarding internal AD zones to DCs): smaller attack surface on the DCs, room for PDNS/RPZ and DoH capacity, and alignment with NIST and DISA role separation. The costs are more infrastructure and the need for conditional forwarding or stub zones toward the DCs.
cut WAN traffic but add another layer of caching and TTL to manage.
NIST’s “dedicated DNS” recommendation and Microsoft’s DNS-on-DC model are the main tension (see below).
Which protective features are built in from the start.
DISA requires Windows DNS response rate limiting to be enabled (V-259417), and requires that the server cannot be used to launch DoS attacks. NIST lists DoS and resource exhaustion as threats.
Cache locking prevents cached records from being overwritten for a percentage of their TTL. The default is 100%.
The socket pool randomizes source ports. It is on by default with 2,500 sockets, configurable from 0 to 10,000.
Both defend against cache poisoning. Keep the defaults.
Disable or limit them to listed secondaries, and authenticate them (NIST, DISA). For AD-only zones, transfers can usually be turned off entirely.
NIST says to keep HINFO, RP, LOC and similar records out of zones that face the internet, and to judge TXT records case by case.
DISA says HINFO, RP, TXT and LOC must not be used in the zone SOA, and the server must refuse version queries.
Disable WINS lookups on the DNS server (DISA).
Microsoft DNS policies support split-brain, recursion scopes (selective recursion by interface or subnet) and query filtering. DoH queries cannot be matched by transport-protocol filters.
The CIS Windows Server 2022 Benchmark v4.0.0 sets:
18.6.4.2 “Configure NetBIOS settings” = Disable NetBIOS name resolution on public networks
18.6.4.4 “Turn off multicast name resolution” = Enabled (disables LLMNR)
Older CIS text adds that NetBIOS over TCP/IP should also be disabled per NIC to fully mitigate name-resolution poisoning.
DISA Windows Server STIGs contain equivalent OS hardening; the exact rule IDs for the DNS client were not verified in this research.

Removing these fallbacks means DNS must be complete. For legacy single-label needs, use GlobalNames or DNS suffix search lists rather than WINS. Microsoft Support KB5071836 (November 2025) states that Windows Server 2025 will be the final LTSC release to include and support WINS, with standard support through November 2034.
NIST says to harden the host operating system. DISA requires zone files and keys to be writable only by the DNS service and administrators, and requires FIPS- validated cryptography.
RRL can drop legitimate bursts from NATed clients, so tune exemptions.
Fully disabling NetBIOS can break legacy applications. CIS’s “public networks only” setting is a compromise; stricter environments disable it everywhere.
CIS’s partial NetBIOS setting is less strict than the full disable that hardening guides commonly recommend. Organizations covered by both CIS and DISA should adopt the stricter one.
What DNS telemetry to capture, how long to keep it, and how to correlate it.
events (configuration changes to zones, records and server) are on by default and have negligible cost.

events (every query and response, via ETW) are off by default. Microsoft Learn’s “Enable DNS Logging and Diagnostics” page cites a 5% performance degradation at 100,000 QPS on modern hardware and “no apparent performance impact” at 50,000 QPS or below.
logging to a file is heavier and is meant for troubleshooting.
DoH has its own analytic events.
The Sentinel “Windows DNS Events via AMA” connector streams only analytic events.
Log current and historical DNS traffic for incident response.
log queries and responses that protective DNS classifies as malicious.
You may filter known-good domains before sending to the SIEM, but keep a complete log for forensics. dnstap or selective logging are options at scale.
Integrate PDNS logs with the SIEM.
Check validator logs for DNSSEC failures.
Use authenticated time (NTS) on signers, validators and encrypted-DNS servers.
AU-8 requires timestamps from internal clocks, in UTC or with a fixed or recorded offset. AU-8(1) and AU-8(2) have been moved to SC- 45(1) and SC-45(2).
SC-45 requires clocks to be synchronized; SC-45(1) adds an authoritative source and SC-45(2) a secondary source in another region.
SC-45 is not in the 800-53B baselines; it appears in the SP 800-82r3 OT overlays.
The DNS server log must be enabled.
The “Manage auditing and security log” right is limited.
Back up audit records at least every seven days to a different system.
Notify administrators of DNSSEC/TSIG failures and anomalies in signed transfers.
8.4 standardizes time synchronization, 8.6 collects DNS query audit logs, 8.9 centralizes logs, and 8.10 retains them.
Analytic logging on busy DCs costs CPU and storage, and the default circular ETL behaviour can drop events. Forward events in near real time with an agent rather than relying on local retention.
Logging at the PDNS forwarder catches egress but loses client attribution behind the forwarder. NIST discusses putting RPZ “closest to the client” versus “closest to the internet” for this reason.
Encrypted DNS removes passive network visibility, so log at the resolver.
None of substance. The sources differ only in prescriptiveness: DISA sets a fixed 7- day backup interval, while NIST and CIS leave retention to organizational policy.

rows: NIST SP 800-81r3: not recommended unless required; of limited value where servers are both authoritative and recursive
DISA STIG: DNSSEC records required, NSEC3 for internal zones, NRPT validation; NIST SP 800-53 SC-20(2) (internal artifacts) isoptional and in no baseline
A real conflict. DoD systems follow DISA; others can follow NIST.
Microsoft: AD- integrated DNS on DCs (secure update only works there)
NIST: dedicated DNS servers; DISA: role separation, and authoritative serversforward only to non- AD-integrated resolvers or DoD ERS
Common middle ground: DCs remain authoritative for AD zones, and clients usededicated resolvers or PDNS that conditionally forward to the DCs.
Microsoft default: root hints, with fallback when forwarders fail
CISA: FCEB must route all outbound DNS to CISA PDNS; NIST: block outbound DNS exceptauthorized forwarders; DISA: root hints only to theinternal root

spans.t: This DNS source collection has been scoped to US sources — official Microsoft guidance plus US government guidance (NIST, CISA/OMB/NSA, DISA, CIS) and the US-based IETF and ICANN — to match the rest of this compendium. Non-US government source sections (UK NCSC, Australia ASD/ACSC, Canada/CCCS, France ANSSI, Germany BSI, EU ENISA) and their crosswalk columns were removed from the broader multi-country collection they were drawn from. A separate standalone US DNS source document also exists but could not be merged from this session.

There is now a clear common baseline across the authorities. NIST SP 800-81r3 (final, March 2026), US federal mandates, DISA and Microsoft’s own documentation all point to five things: DNSSEC, restricted recursion, protected dynamic updates and zone transfers, protective DNS/filtering, and query logging. They split mainly on how to encrypt DNS (DoH vs DoT, and whether to encrypt inside the network) and on how much logging is required. This collection verifies the preliminary items against publisher pages where possible, corrects several of them, and states plainly what could not be re-verified.

Server-side DNS over HTTPS for the Windows Server 2025 DNS Server role became generally available with the June 9, 2026 update (KB5094125). It covers client-to-server traffic only: forwarders, zone transfers and dynamic updates stay unencrypted. An older Microsoft Learn page still warns against “Require DoH” on domain-joined clients because the DNS Server role “doesn’t support DoH queries”, which is now outdated.
Protective DNS there is one of three acceptable mitigations, not a standalone mandate.

Document the timing topology, including which servers distribute time and their traceability to stratum-1.

Members and member servers sync from a DC in their domain; DCs sync from DCs, including the PDC emulator of their own domain; a child domain’s PDC emulator syncs up the hierarchy into the parent or forest root. Only the forest-root PDC emulator, or an explicitly configured reliable DC or appliance, should hold an external peer list.

The W32Time settings that make the forest-root PDC emulator authoritative are local registry or GPO values on that server; they do not travel with the FSMO role. After a transfer or seizure, the design must point the new role holder at external peers (
. A common pattern is a GPO scoped by a WMI filter to the current PDC emulator; this is community practice, with no Microsoft or DISA mandate for it.

The default hierarchy needs almost no configuration and gives Kerberos-grade consistency; its weak point is one key server that must be reconfigured whenever the role moves. Manual peer lists on members break the “single source of truth” and trigger STIG findings unless the peers are DoD-approved. AllSync has no clear design rationale in the sources and is rarely used.
None of substance. Microsoft and DISA describe the same hierarchy, and DISA adds the DoD-source constraint.
What does the top of the hierarchy sync from, and how many sources?
; plus authenticated servers for DoD NIPRNet customers only.
(routers/firewalls/appliances that authenticate to NIST or USNO and re-serve internally).
(f) The community pool.ntp.org, or vendor services such as
; hard-coding a particular server name/address is “a bad practice”; clients must never query more than once every 4 seconds.

The stratum-1 servers are open to stratum-2 servers in the same time zone; individual users should use public stratum-2 servers. USNO “strongly recommend[s]” picking one or more nearby servers plus others for redundancy. DoD entities should use only the DoD authenticated USNO servers, not the public hosts. USNO notes Windows lacks a symmetric-key NTP client and advises authenticating to USNO on routers/firewalls and having Windows sync from those devices.
The forest-root PDC emulator and any
system must use a DoD time source; the fix text points to the USNO/CNMOC NTP pages.

Network time must be synchronized “to a traceable time source designated within the agency”; agencies are encouraged to use sources traceable to USNO or NIST where feasible. The memo excludes national security systems and DoD/IC systems.
UTC(USNO) and UTC(NIST) are the principal official US time sources; use “at least two or more traceable time sources with the lowest possible stratum”; diversify receiver types and sources.
Network devices should use at least two NTP servers, with NTP authentication enabled.
“Configure at least two synchronized time sources across enterprise assets, where supported” (IG2/IG3). Version 7.1 had asked for three.
Use at least four independent, diverse sources; two cannot resolve a disagreement between them.
Since Server 2016’s algorithm changes, use three or more time servers; with only two, flag one
(0x2). The STS article adds that “an odd number of comparable time servers (more than one)” helps redundancy.
A volunteer, community service with no US-government standing; under DISA rules not a DoD source, and it does not give the documented traceability OMB asks for. Common in non-regulated environments.

NIST/USNO public servers give documented traceability at no cost but are unauthenticated over the internet and rate-limited (and USNO restricts its stratum-1 servers to stratum-2 servers). A GPS appliance gives internet independence and low stratum but brings GNSS spoofing/jamming risk and firmware-lifecycle work (CISA cites the 2019 GPS week- rollover failures). More sources improve fault detection but need more firewall egress and monitoring.

Source count: two (CIS, NSA, CISA), three/odd (Microsoft), four (IETF). DoD vs civilian: DoD must use USNO or an approved DoD source; civilian agencies under OMB are only “encouraged” toward USNO/NIST traceability.
What accuracy does the estate need, and what will it cost to support?
Default Kerberos-grade time; 1 s; 50 ms; 1 ms. Beyond 1 ms, non-W32Time solutions (PTP-capable third-party software or appliances) are needed.
What Microsoft says (Support boundary page, updated 2026-02-12).
W32Time only gave Kerberos-grade, “loosely accurate” time; tighter accuracy was unsupported.
can deliver 1 s, 50 ms or 1 ms “under the right operating conditions.” Accuracy depends on an accurate, stable stratum-1 root and the end-to-end path; asymmetry or high CPU load degrades it.

Windows 10 / Server 2016+; an NTP hierarchy ending in a highly accurate, Windows-compatible source; every node configured per “Configuring Systems for High Accuracy”; cumulative one-way latency of 100 ms or less.
latency under 5 ms to the source; stratum 5 or less; six or fewer hops; one-day average CPU of 90% or less on every stratum (and the host for VMs).
latency under 0.1 ms; stratum 5 or less; four or fewer hops; CPU 80% or less (including host).
“most customers don’t require highly accurate time.” The default aims to satisfy Kerberos v5 and loosely accurate time; higher tiers require registry/GPO changes (polling intervals, update rates).

CISA: validate whether applications really need time and at what accuracy relative to UTC(NIST)/UTC(USNO) (its example: trading firms timestamping within 50 µs). USNO: typical internet NTP accuracy is 1–30 ms. NIST SP 800-53 AU-8: leaves timestamp granularity to the organization.

Each AD tier (forest-root PDC, child PDC, DC, member) adds a stratum; a deep multi-domain forest can hit the stratum-5 limit for the 50 ms and 1 ms tiers. Shallow hierarchies or appliances near consumers address this.

Higher tiers need tighter polling (more traffic and DC load), latency engineering, CPU headroom and monitoring. Regulated sectors (finance, telecom, energy) are the usual drivers; for most AD estates, the default plus good sources and monitoring is enough.
None. Other authorities leave the accuracy target to the organization and do not contradict Microsoft’s tiers.
What clock-skew tolerance is acceptable, and how does time sync protect authentication?

“Maximum tolerance for computer clock synchronization” sets the maximum difference Kerberos v5 tolerates between client and KDC clocks; Microsoft advises 5 minutes (also the default). It lives in the Default Domain Policy under Account Policies > Kerberos Policy. W32Time was originally built to meet the Kerberos requirement that clocks be synchronized.

WS2022: V-254390 / WN22-DC-000060 (Medium). WS2025: V-278137 / WN25-DC-000060 (Medium). Both require the setting to be 5 minutes or less; the Windows Server STIG time rules justify time sync as “essential for authentication and auditing purposes.”
Inaccurate forest time can cause access to resources on computers with accurate time to be denied, and weakens audit data as forensic evidence.

Kerberos ticket issuance and replay protection depend on time, and so does everything built on Kerberos (Group Policy, LDAP and SMB authentication). X.509 certificate validity windows and token lifetimes depend on it too. Separately, large backward time jumps on DCs can cause replication problems (Microsoft’s virtualization guidance cites lingering objects and replication stopping).
: default 172,800 s (48 h) on DCs and 0xFFFFFFFF on domain members (corrections larger than these are logged rather than applied).
: default 300 s on domain members (offsets above it are stepped rather than slewed).
Raising the tolerance hides time faults and widens the replay window; lowering it below 5 minutes increases authentication failures when time degrades.
None. Microsoft’s default and DISA’s maximum are the same.
Should virtualized DCs take time from the hypervisor or from the AD hierarchy?
In Hyper-V, clear the “Time synchronization” integration service with the VM off.
Leave the integration service on (guest gets correct time at boot/restore) but set
so W32Time ignores the host as a source.
Other hypervisors have equivalent “sync guest time with host” settings.
Microsoft (Virtualizing DCs with Hyper-V): disable time sync between host and guest for VMs acting as DCs so the DC syncs from the domain hierarchy. Microsoft AskDS (2024): disable
on DCs and other VMs that should follow the AD hierarchy; check with

(“VM IC Time Synchronization Provider” in the output means the host is the source). Microsoft (STS article): VM hosts are time-sensitive machines where STS should be disabled, and the host’s own clock should come from a reliable source. Older Microsoft guidance suggested leaving host sync on and later moved to “partial disable”; the current Learn page resolves this by recommending host sync be disabled for DCs.

Full disable removes the conflict between two time authorities but the VM may boot with a stale clock after save/restore until W32Time corrects it within phase-correction limits. Partial disable keeps boot-time seeding but Windows updates or integration-service resets can re-enable the provider, so it needs monitoring. The forest-root PDC emulator as a VM is a special case: it must not take host time, and its host should itself be synced to a reliable source.
None among current documents; the conflict is only historical.
How is the integrity of time protected, inside the forest and at the external boundary?

Symmetric-key NTP (RFC 5905 MAC) — pre-shared key/key ID with MD5, SHA- 1 or SHA-2 digest, manual key management. NTS (RFC 8915) — TLS-based key establishment (NTS-KE on TCP 4460), then authenticated NTP on UDP 123, automatic key management, scales. Autokey (RFC 5906) — known vulnerabilities; RFC 8633 says “Autokey SHOULD NOT be used.” Inside AD, W32Time protects time samples with domain security extensions (MS-SNTP using the Netlogon secure channel); Microsoft describes AD as “NTP augmented with ADDS security extensions within the AD domain/forest,” and “typically bridged outside the AD forest through standard plaintext NTP.”

It does not implement NTS; it does not implement symmetric-key client authentication to standard NTP servers (USNO states this explicitly). So any external peer configured on the forest-root PDC emulator is unauthenticated.

Free, symmetric key, IPv4 only; request by US mail or fax listing up to four static IPv4 addresses; key types MD5, SHA1, SHA256, HMAC-SHA256, SHA3-256; NIST never sends keys by email; unused keys (no use over a 30-day window at the annual survey) are deleted without notice; NAT/proxies complicate registration; NIST does not support Autokey and does “not yet” support NTS-KE.

Symmetric-key authentication offered only to DoD on NIPRNet, by signed-email request (SHA256 recommended; MD5/SHA1 legacy); the public service has no authentication. The DoD page still says NTS is “coming soon,” projected for NIPRNet in “1QTR 2025” — a date that has passed with no update, so current availability is unconfirmed.

NSA: enable NTP authentication on all network devices, strong unique keys, at least two servers. CISA: have an authentication scheme to verify time comes from legitimate servers, and block non-authenticated ports at the perimeter. RFC 8633: do not use Autokey; NTS is the replacement.
What is achievable on an all-Windows estate.

(1) Rely on AD’s built-in authenticated distribution inside the forest. (2) Terminate authenticated upstream time on a non-Windows component the forest-root PDC emulator then syncs from over plaintext NTP on a trusted segment — routers/firewalls with NIST/USNO or other symmetric keys; GPS/stratum-1 appliances; Linux chrony/NTPsec using NTS or symmetric keys (USNO itself recommends this pattern). (3) Add egress filtering so only designated time hosts reach external UDP 123. (4) Monitor for time jumps.

Symmetric keys are mature but need manual key handling and IPv4 registration with NIST; NTS scales but neither W32Time nor (yet) NIST/USNO public service supports it; the intermediary pattern adds components that must be inventoried and patched (CISA stresses timing devices in lifecycle management).
IETF, NSA and CISA expect authenticated time, but the Microsoft time service cannot provide it externally. This is the main standing gap in this reference.
Should STS be enabled on servers?
A heuristic in W32Time that estimates the current time from metadata in outbound SSL/TLS connections and uses it to correct large clock errors. Controlled by
(registry or GPO under Windows Time Service > Global Configuration Settings); needs a reboot to change.

Enabled by default on all editions of Windows Server 2016, 2019 and 2022, and on Windows 10 1511+ and Windows 11 clients. Disabled by default on Windows Server 2025, “based on customer feedback.” The Tools and Settings registry reference confirms default 1 everywhere except Server 2025 (0); domain membership does not change it. Note: the GPO “Global Configuration Settings” default table still lists
when the policy is enabled, so enabling that GPO on Server 2025 without setting the value explicitly could re-enable STS (an inference from the published defaults, not a Microsoft statement).

Disable STS on Windows Server machines with time-sensitive workloads, explicitly including AD DS domain controllers and VM hosts; consider disabling it on all Windows Server machines even if no problems have been seen. The reported failures were random time jumps of days to years (some self-corrected, some persisted). Roll out gradually, test first, and confirm the setting through events 257, 260 or 263, or the W32Time debug log; put time monitoring in place (e.g., Kernel-General Event 1) before and after. The guidance is not extended to client SKUs.

by GPO, at minimum on DCs and hypervisor hosts. Server 2025: verify the value rather than assume it. Clients: leave STS at default unless problems appear (some devices, e.g., with flat CMOS batteries, rely on STS to recover).
Disabling STS removes a source of unexplained time jumps on servers; it also removes a recovery path for machines that boot with grossly wrong time and cannot reach NTP, so monitoring compensates.
None among US authorities. STIG and CIS coverage of STS was not verified for this report.
How is time health monitored, how are log timestamps standardized, and how are leap seconds handled?
(domain-wide offsets; prefix a computer name with
Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service events (source changes logged by default,

=2); events 257, 260 and 263 record configuration including STS state; Kernel- General Event 1 records every system-time change and the process that made it; commonly cited W32Time warnings include no-usable-source and unsynchronized-for-extended-period events (exact IDs not verified against a current Microsoft page);

NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-8: audit records carry timestamps from internal clocks at an organization-defined granularity, using UTC, a fixed UTC offset, or an embedded offset; the synchronization enhancements AU-8(1)/(2) were withdrawn and moved to SC-45(1) (authoritative source) and SC-45(2) (secondary authoritative source). DISA maps its time rules to AU-8(1)/SC-45(1). CIS Control 8.4 treats time sync as part of audit log management. OMB M-26-14 Appendix B: logs “must include a consistently accurate timestamp”; network time via NTP or equivalent to an agency-designated traceable source, preferably traceable to USNO or NIST. CISA/NSA/FBI joint event-logging guidance (Aug 2024): set up an accurate, trustworthy time source and use it consistently, with the same date-time format everywhere; use multiple sources where possible; prefer UTC. CISA: timestamps and correctly correlated offsets are critical to reconstructing intrusion timelines. NIST SP 800-92: broader log-management planning, including clock consistency across log sources.

Windows: W32Time historically “does not implement a leap second” — it passes the NTP Leap Indicator downstream but does not insert the second and corrects through normal sync; the same archived Microsoft page (KB2722715) states WS2019 and Windows 10 October 2018 Update support leap seconds in the platform. Dissemination: NIST and USNO disseminate leap-second information, and NTP carries leap warnings (NIST lists this as a protocol feature); NIST publishes a leap-seconds data file (current location not re-verified). CISA: test before and after known time events such as leap seconds and DST, and document how systems handle them. CGPM status: in 2022 the 27th CGPM (Resolution 4) decided to raise the UT1–UTC tolerance by or before 2035; at the 28th CGPM on 15 October 2026, delegates adopted Resolution 5 (“On the technical actions needed to ensure the continuity of UTC”), under which “continuous UTC will become effective on 20 May 2027” and the maximum |UT1– UTC| becomes 3,600 seconds (1 hour), per the BIPM-published resolution text. The last leap second was 31 December 2016; no negative leap second has ever been applied.

Monitor and alert on offset against designated references, and on time- jump events; standardize log timestamps on UTC; keep leap-second handling in test plans until May 2027, then treat leap seconds as a legacy concern while keeping code paths tolerant.
None material. The authorities differ only in how strongly they mandate UTC: CISA/NSA prefer it, while NIST also allows a fixed or embedded offset.

blocks.text: Where authorities agree, differ, or conflict

spans.t: The forest-root PDC emulator is the external boundary (Microsoft, DISA). Time must be traceable to national standards; UTC(NIST) and UTC(USNO) are the official US references (CISA, OMB, DISA). Use more than one upstream source. Kerberos tolerance stays at 5 minutes or less (Microsoft, DISA). Synchronized time is required for logging and forensics (NIST, OMB, CISA/NSA, CIS, DISA). Virtualized DCs must not take host time (Microsoft). Autokey should not be used (IETF; NIST does not support it).

Number of sources: CIS, NSA and CISA say at least two; Microsoft says three or more (or an odd number), with two as a fallback configuration; IETF says four or more. Default accuracy vs high accuracy: Microsoft’s default only promises Kerberos-grade time; CISA and NIST leave granularity to the organization; regulated workloads need the 50 ms or 1 ms tiers and their conditions. Direct NIST/USNO vs internal hierarchy: NIST encourages

and discourages hard-coding; USNO restricts its stratum-1 servers to stratum-2 servers; DISA requires DoD sources; all three favor syncing only the top of an internal hierarchy externally. pool.ntp.org: acceptable as community context but not a US-government source (does not satisfy DISA; weaker documented traceability than OMB prefers). Leap seconds: NIST and USNO historically disseminate them, while Windows historically does not insert them; the October 2026 CGPM decision ends new leap seconds from 20 May 2027.

W32Time vs authenticated-time guidance: NSA and CISA call for authenticated NTP, and IETF points to NTS; NIST offers only symmetric-key (and no NTS yet); USNO offers authentication only to DoD; W32Time supports neither symmetric-key nor NTS to external servers. USNO’s own workaround (authenticate on network devices) is the only US- government-documented answer. Secure Time Seeding defaults: Microsoft ships STS enabled on Server 2016–2022 but recommends disabling it on servers; it changed the default only in Server 2025; meanwhile the GPO default table still shows 1, a source of configuration drift.

The 15 Oct 2026 CGPM decision (Resolution 5; effective 20 May 2027; maximum |UT1–UTC| of 3,600 s) is taken from the BIPM-published resolution text; NIST/USNO post-decision notices were not checked.

Specific W32Time recommendation numbers and values were not verified for this report; they are commonly “Enable Windows NTP Client = Enabled,” with the NTP Server setting varying by profile. Check the current benchmark for your OS version.
NIST CSRC lists Rev 1 as an Initial Public Draft (11 Oct 2023) that will replace the 2006 Final version once finalized.

That the W32Time external configuration does not follow a PDC role transfer is standard practice and follows from W32Time being configured per machine; no single current Microsoft page states it verbatim. GPO/WMI-filter automation is community practice.

Applies to federal civilian agencies; national security systems and DoD/IC systems are excluded, so DoD estates follow DISA/USNO instead. The joint event-logging guide was led by Australia’s ASD ACSC and co-sealed by CISA, NSA and FBI; it is used here only as a US co-authored source.

catalog.title: US Reference Collection: NTP and Time Synchronization for Windows/Enterprise Environments (verified October 2026)

spans.t: The US baseline is consistent across sources. Inside an Active Directory forest, time flows down a hierarchy from the forest-root PDC emulator, and that PDC emulator should take time from an authoritative external source such as NIST, USNO (US Naval Observatory), GPS or a stratum- 1 appliance. Kerberos tolerates 5 minutes of clock skew. Most items from the prior pass held up, but several were wrong or out of date: STIG severities, NIST authenticated-server details, the leap-second timeline, how W32Time authenticates, and the USNO page URLs.
The domain hierarchy is NT5DS. The forest-root PDC emulator is the root and syncs to an external NTP source.
The Kerberos skew policy is 5 minutes.

Secure Time Seeding (STS) is on by default in Server 2016/2019/2022 and off by default in Server 2025. Microsoft recommends disabling it on time-sensitive servers such as DCs and VM hosts, and suggests considering it for all Windows Server machines.
Up to 1 ms accuracy is supported only on Windows 10 / Server 2016 or later, and only under strict network, stratum and CPU conditions.

W32Time documents no support for NTS (RFC 8915). Its only built-in authentication works inside the domain and is signed with Kerberos/Net Logon session keys. Manually configured external peers are unauthenticated.
The US government baseline is “sync to an authoritative source, with redundancy”:
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-8 covers timestamps. Synchronization moved from AU-8(1)/(2) to SC-45(1)/(2).

OMB Memorandum M-26-14 (22 May 2026) rescinded M-21-31. It requires log timestamps synchronized by NTP or equivalent “to a traceable time source designated within the agency”, and encourages sources traceable to USNO or NIST.
DISA STIGs require a DoD source. AD Forest V-243504 (forest-root PDC external source) is CAT II. The Windows Server 2022/2025 “DOD time source” rules are CAT III (Low).
CIS Safeguard 8.4 requires at least two synchronized time sources.
NSA recommends at least two NTP servers plus NTP authentication on network devices.
Live services, checked on publisher pages:
NIST ITS lists 20+ stratum-1 hostnames behind time.nist.gov and a “never more than once every 4 seconds” rule.
NIST’s symmetric-key authenticated servers are ntp-b, ntp-wwv and ntp-d. They are free but need a mailed or faxed request and registered static IPv4 addresses.
USNO publishes tick/tock/ntp2.usno.navy.mil as public servers on its CNMOC site. It tells DoD entities not to use them and to use its authenticated DoD servers instead.

On 15 October 2026 the 28th CGPM (the General Conference on Weights and Measures) adopted Resolution 5, which makes UTC continuous from 20 May 2027. This ends leap seconds earlier than the 2022 “by 2035” resolution. A BIPM statement by CCTF President Noël Dimarcq says “continuous UTC will take effect on 20 May 2027” and sets “a long-term limit of one hour” for UTC−UT1.

systems before Windows 10 1607 / Server 2016 1607 “can’t guarantee highly accurate time”. They were designed only for Kerberos- level accuracy.

The content is Server 2016-era but still the current publication.
A3. Secure Time Seeding recommendations for Windows Server
STS is “enabled by default in all editions of Windows Server 2016, Windows Server 2019, and Windows Server 2022”, and in Windows clients from Windows 10 version 1511 onward.
It is “disabled by default in Windows Server 2025, based on customer feedback”.

A4. Maximum tolerance for computer clock synchronization
This is a Kerberos policy. It sets “the maximum time difference (in minutes) that Kerberos V5 tolerates” between client and DC clocks.
The current page advises 5 minutes. The legacy Server 2003 page states the policy “is set to 5 minutes by default” and explains the replay-attack rationale.
A5. Windows Time service tools and settings

A6. How the Windows Time Service works; AD time hierarchy
W32Time “isn’t an exact implementation” of NTP. Its NTP provider “follows the standards specified by NTP version 3”. It does not support broadcast or multicast peers.
In a forest, the forest-root PDC emulator “holds the position of best time source, unless another reliable time source has been configured”.
The first DC is automatically a reliable source and should sync externally.
The PDC emulator of a child domain can sync from the parent domain.
DCs are scored as follows: same site 8, reliable 4, parent domain 2, PDC emulator 1.

the external configuration does not follow the role. This comes from the legacy Server 2008 R2 page “Configuring a time source for the forest”, which tells admins to reconfigure both old and new PDC emulators when the role moves. As an alternative, it suggests configuring a non-PDC DC in the forest root as the reliable source. I found no current Learn page restating this, so treat it as legacy-sourced.
packets are signed with the computer’s Kerberos session key, managed by Net Logon. Unsigned or badly signed replies are rejected.
“Manually specified time sources are not authenticated unless a specific time provider is written for them”. Cross-forest sync “is not secure”.

no Microsoft page documents NTS (RFC 8915) support. Microsoft also documents no RFC 5905 symmetric-key (key ID / MAC) configuration for W32Time’s external peers. Autokey is not mentioned. NIST’s authenticated servers do not support Autokey either.
