design.title: Part IV — US Design Reference: Windows Enterprise PKI with Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) (as of October 2026)
areas: CA protection, role separation, auditing and key-backup design

spans.t: The US design baseline for AD CS across Microsoft, CISA/NSA and DISA comes down to five points: build at least a two-tier hierarchy with an offline standalone root; treat every CA and its backups as Tier 0 assets; keep CA keys in an HSM; tightly scope certificate templates (no enrollee-supplied subject for authentication certificates unless a CA manager approves the request); and design certificate-based logon around strong (SID-based) mapping and NTAuth chaining, both of which Microsoft now enforces with no registry bypass. Microsoft supplies the architecture mechanics, CISA/NSA the threat-driven controls, and DISA the binary compliance rules. NIST and NSA set the cryptographic clock: SHA-1 out by 2030, quantum-vulnerable RSA/ECDSA deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035 (still a draft), and CNSA 2.0 for National Security Systems. That clock now meets a real product milestone, because AD CS on Windows Server 2025 gained ML-DSA issuance in May 2026.
Use an offline standalone root CA, plus one or more online enterprise subordinate (issuing) CAs.
Add a policy/intermediate tier only when there is a concrete policy, legal or delegation need. Microsoft-published guidance calls the middle tier “often never utilized”.
Configure CDP/AIA (HTTP first) before the first certificate is issued.
Renew CA certificates at half-life. Avoid delta CRLs on offline roots.
Treat AD CS as Tier 0 and manage it only from Tier 0 PAWs/jump hosts with dedicated CA admin accounts (DISA V-269099, CAT I).
Protect CA keys with an HSM, which CISA/NSA list as a control that “should be implemented”.
Encrypt CA backups and restrict them to Backup Administrators.
Turn on full CA auditing and forward the logs centrally.
Remove the “enrollee supplies subject” flag from authentication templates, or require CA certificate manager approval for them. DISA V-269098 (CAT I) makes manual approval mandatory for certain EKUs.
Mitigate ESC8 relay with HTTPS + Extended Protection for Authentication and by disabling NTLM (KB5005413).
Strong certificate mapping (KB5014754) has been fully enforced since September 9, 2025.
NTAuth chaining for Kerberos certificate logon (KB5057784 / CVE-2025-26647) has been enforced with no bypass since October 14, 2025.
Use SHA-256 or stronger. NIST’s draft SP 800-131A Rev. 3 would disallow SHA-1 after 2030.

Plan new hierarchies for crypto-agility: RSA-3072/4096 or P-384 today, and a parallel ML-DSA hierarchy for testing. NIST IR 8547 (draft) proposes deprecating quantum-vulnerable algorithms after 2030 and disallowing them after 2035. NSA CNSA 2.0 requires ML-DSA-87 for National Security Systems.

Status is as of October 19, 2026. Licence notes: US federal works (NIST, CISA, NSA, DISA) are generally public domain in the US, though third-party content and logos are excluded. Microsoft Learn/Support content falls under Microsoft Terms of Use; Microsoft Learn documentation text is also published on GitHub under CC BY 4.0, but verify per page. CIS Controls/Benchmarks are free for non-commercial use under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, with commercial use requiring CIS SecureSuite membership. IETF RFCs fall under the IETF Trust Legal Provisions, which allow free reproduction of the full text. CA/Browser Forum documents are freely published under the Forum’s IPR policy. Practitioner papers are copyrighted by their authors. Everything listed is free to access unless noted.

Standalone CAs do not use templates; their CRLs and CA certificates “must be manually published into Active Directory.” An offline root should therefore be standalone and non-domain-joined; the archived table rates an offline enterprise root as an uncommon configuration “with no known benefit.”

CAs should do nothing but AD CS — “do not install any non-security-related services or applications” — and should use application control. These favour dedicated servers over co-locating the CA role with domain controllers; Microsoft’s archived table likewise lists “Enterprise root CA on a domain controller” as the weakest option.
V-269099 requires AD CS servers to be managed only from Tier 0 PAWs, implying enterprise (domain-joined) issuing CAs sit inside the Tier 0 boundary.

enterprise CAs bring automation (templates, autoenrollment, SID extension, NTAuth publication) but also AD-wide attack surface (template ACLs, the ESC paths). Standalone CAs reduce AD dependency but need manual approval and publication. key algorithm and size; hash algorithm; provider and key protection; CA key lifetime relative to algorithm strength; FIPS; post-quantum readiness.
RSA-2048/-3072/-4096; ECDSA P-256/P-384 via a CNG KSP; SHA-256/-384/- 512; software KSP, network/PCIe HSM, or TPM-backed keys for end entities; ML-DSA-44/-65/- 87 on WS2025.

choose the provider, hash and key length after checking “what cryptographic options the applications and devices that you intend to use can support.” Legacy CSPs support only SHA-1/MD-family hashes; the Microsoft Software KSP supports SHA-256/384/512 and ECDSA — so new CAs should use a CNG KSP. An HSM must be installed before the CA is configured if CA keys are to live on it. Microsoft’s sample root CAPolicy.inf uses

suggests “a maximum cryptoperiod of about one to three years” for a private signature key; for certified keys, the cryptoperiod ends at the notAfter of the last certificate issued for that key, and the validity periods of the original and all renewed certificates “shall not extend beyond” the key’s cryptoperiod. NIST calls these “rough order-of-magnitude guidelines.” The 1–3-year figure is far shorter than typical 10–20-year root lifetimes; no NIST document sets a separate CA-key cryptoperiod.

Rev. 2 (final) governs 112-bit minimum security (RSA- 2048/P-224+). The Rev. 3 draft would deprecate SHA-1 and 224-bit hashes “through December 31, 2030” and disallow them thereafter, moving toward 128-bit security. NIST’s 2022 announcement says SHA-1 will be retired for all applications by December 31, 2030.
NIST IR 8547 (initial public draft, Nov 12, 2024; still draft):
proposes deprecating quantum- vulnerable public-key algorithms at 112-bit strength after 2030 and disallowing all quantum- vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2035.
covers stateful hash-based signatures (LMS/XMSS), suited to firmware signing, not general CA use.

ML-DSA-87 for signatures, ML-KEM-1024, AES-256, SHA-384/512, LMS/XMSS for software/firmware signing. New NSS acquisitions must be CNSA 2.0-compliant from January 1, 2027; most categories must use CNSA 2.0 exclusively by 2033, with all NSS quantum-resistant by 2035. Secondary summaries say ML-DSA-44/-65 are not acceptable for NSS.
EO 14412 / OMB M-26-15 (June 2026, federal civilian agencies):

secondary analyses report EO 14412 requires agencies to migrate their most sensitive systems to PQC for key establishment by December 31, 2030 and to PQC for digital signatures by December 31, 2031, with M-26-15 setting a January 2, 2030 deadline for TLS 1.3; agency migration plans are due within 120 days of M-26-15 (reported as about October 22, 2026). These bind federal agencies, not private enterprises.

AD CS on Windows Server 2025 supports ML-DSA. Microsoft Learn gives the minimum version as “Windows Server 2025 with the 2026- 05 Security update (KB5087539) or later,” supports all three ML-DSA parameter sets in pure mode, and states existing RSA/ECC CAs cannot be converted: “ML-DSA doesn’t support in-place migration of existing CAs. Build a new CA hierarchy in parallel with your existing hierarchy.” PQC is available only through CNG providers.
“Use a HSM to protect key material for AD CS CAs … the private key for CAs cannot be backed up and exfiltrated.”
and the DISA Windows Server STIGs govern protocol/algorithm configuration of the hosts; they do not set CA key sizes.

RSA-4096 roots and RSA-2048/3072 issuing CAs maximize compatibility; P-384 is smaller and CNSA 1.0-aligned, but some legacy devices and smart cards lack ECC support. Larger keys and HSMs add cost and latency. ML-DSA certificates are much larger (per Microsoft Learn, an ML-DSA-87 signature is 4,627 bytes vs 2,420 for ML-DSA-44), clients need Windows 11 24H2/25H2 with the 2025-10 update, and NDES enrollment “isn’t currently available” — so parallel ML-DSA hierarchies are a test/pilot track in 2026, not a replacement.
CA certificate lifetimes; when to renew and whether to re-key; end-entity lifetimes; how CRL periods interact with renewal.

“CAs can’t issue certificates that are valid beyond their own validity period.” “A best practice is to renew the CA certificate when half of its validity period is expired.” CAPolicy.inf controls renewal (
); Microsoft’s sample root uses 20 years. An issuing CA’s effective issuance window shrinks as its own certificate approaches expiry; renewal at half-life preserves full- length end-entity issuance.
renewing a CA certificate on the same key cannot extend total validity beyond that key’s cryptoperiod — so the design favours re-keying at renewal over indefinite key reuse.
for TLS server certificates, maintain an inventory, monitor continuously, automate renewal; executives should “establish formal TLS server certificate management programs.”

Ballot SC- 081v3 caps publicly trusted TLS certificates at 200 days from March 15, 2026, 100 days from March 15, 2027 and 47 days from March 15, 2029. Internal AD CS hierarchies that are not publicly trusted are not bound; browsers enforce the limits only for roots in public trust programs.
defines validity semantics; does not set lifetimes.

long internal lifetimes reduce renewal churn but lengthen exposure if a key is compromised; short lifetimes require autoenrollment, CES/CEP, ACME-style tooling or similar automation. Re-keying at CA renewal creates a new CA certificate and key-index CRLs; clients need both chains during overlap.
CRL only, CRL plus delta CRL, or CRL plus OCSP (Online Responder); HTTP vs LDAP publication and ordering; CRL validity and overlap periods.

configure AIA and CDP extensions “before the CA issues any certificates” — changing a URL affects only newly issued certificates. “Avoid publishing delta CRLs on offline root CAs” (the WS2012 TLG sets

). Publish an HTTP CRL location for external and non-Windows clients. “Windows clients always retrieve the list of URLs in sequential order until a valid CRL is retrieved,” so URL order is a latency/availability decision; common practice lists HTTP before LDAP. Microsoft’s Online Responder implements OCSP and on WS2025 can sign responses with ML-DSA.
RFC 5280 defines CRLs, delta CRLs, CDP and AIA; RFC 6960 defines OCSP; RFC 5019 defines a lightweight, cache-friendly OCSP profile.
stress that rogue or attacker-obtained certificates “remain valid until they are revoked”; revocation must be part of incident response.
No US authority reviewed here mandates OCSP for internal enterprise PKI.
OCSP is optional, justified mainly where CRL size/latency is a problem or relying parties require it.

delta CRLs give fresher data but more publication jobs and failure points; OCSP gives low-latency checks but responder availability and signing-certificate management become their own dependency; LDAP CDPs suit domain clients only and can create site- unaware lookups. On an offline root, CRL validity and overlap must outlast the interval between ceremonies (long root CRL periods are standard; issuing-CA CRLs are typically days).

which template schema versions to use; who can enroll; whether subjects are built from AD or supplied in the request; issuance requirements (manager approval, authorized signatures); EKU/application-policy scope; template lifecycle.

version 2+ templates are editable and support autoenrollment; template permissions (Read, Enroll, Autoenroll) define who can obtain certificates; superseding templates migrate holders (e.g., DC certificates). Archived guidance says to remove unneeded templates from the moment the issuing CA is stood up and to document each template’s issuance requirements and enrollment groups. The TechCommunity hardening blog: “Never allow ‘Enrollee Supplied Subject’ without manager approval.”

CVE-2024-49019 (EKUwu/ESC15, patched Nov 12, 2024) — on schema-version-1 templates that allow a supplied subject, a requester could inject application policies that override the template EKU. Design lesson (practitioner-sourced): avoid publishing v1 templates; duplicating a v1 template creates a v2+ template.

an ESC1-vulnerable template has four properties — low-privilege enrollment, an authentication EKU, a supplied SAN, no manager approval. Mitigations: remove the Enrollee Supplies Subject flag; restrict write permissions on templates; remove the CA flag EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2; require CA Certificate Manager approval where a SAN can be supplied; remove authentication EKUs where not needed. Templates enrollable by Domain Computers are a pathway if attackers can create machine accounts.

templates with certain EKUs must require manual CA approval in all cases, including Smart Card Logon and subordinate-CA certificates; templates with authentication-relevant EKUs that allow “Supply in the request” must also require manual approval. Not a finding if “Supply in the request” is not selected and enroll permissions are limited to a select group.

the ESC1–ESC16 taxonomy. Template-level paths include ESC1/2/3 (supplied subject; any-purpose EKU; enrollment-agent abuse), ESC4 (writable template ACLs), ESC9/10 (weak mapping or no security extension), ESC13 (issuance-policy-to-group links), ESC15 (EKUwu). CA-level paths include ESC6 (SAN flag), ESC7 (CA ACLs), ESC8/11 (relay) and ESC16 (SID security extension disabled CA-wide). Certify 2.0 enumerates ESC1–ESC16.

manager approval is strong but does not scale for high-volume templates; tight enrollment ACLs plus AD-built subjects scale through autoenrollment but depend on ACL hygiene; unpublishing v1 defaults can break legacy workflows unless duplicates are issued first.
which enrollment interfaces to expose (GPO autoenrollment; CA Web Enrollment; CES/CEP; NDES/SCEP; third-party ACME/EST gateways); whether to require key attestation.

autoenrollment (template permissions plus a GPO) is the native domain path; CES/CEP serve non-domain or off-network clients; NDES implements SCEP for devices; TPM key attestation can be required on v4 templates.

Web Enrollment and CES accept NTLM by default and are relay targets. Primary mitigations: “enabling EPA and disabling HTTP on AD CS servers” (enable Extended Protection for Authentication and Require SSL — EPA is ineffective without Require SSL). Further: restrict incoming NTLM on AD CS servers by GPO, disable NTLM in IIS for these role services, and disable NTLM domain-wide where possible.
disable NTLM wherever possible; otherwise enable LDAP channel binding, EPA and SMB signing. Install only the AD CS functions that are needed (remove unused role services such as Web Enrollment).

RFC 8894 (SCEP, Informational) documents weak requester authentication (a shared challenge password), so NDES deployments need tightly scoped templates and challenge handling. RFC 8555 (ACME) is the modern automation model behind public-trust renewal; AD CS has no native ACME server.
ESC8 (HTTP relay) and ESC11 (RPC relay where the CA does not enforce request encryption) are endpoint-design issues, not template issues.

each additional enrollment endpoint widens the attack surface and the Tier 0 boundary; NDES enables device enrollment but concentrates a registration-authority credential (avoid where an MDM/connector with better authentication is available); key attestation raises assurance but requires TPM-capable clients and attestation trust configuration.

each DC should have a certificate based on the Kerberos Authentication template, used as a baseline for an updated “Domain Controller Authentication (Kerberos)” template, which should supersede Domain Controller and Domain Controller Authentication. the WS2025 STIG requires DCs to have a PKI server certificate (V-278159); the OS STIGs require DoD root CA certificates in the Trusted Root store (WS2022 V-254442; WS2025 V-278192, now worded “DoW”).

strong mapping breaks legacy, MDM-issued and third-party smart-card flows that lack the SID (explicit mappings scale poorly); minimizing NTAuth membership reduces risk but requires inventorying every CA used for logon.

blocks.text: 9. CA protection, role separation, auditing and key-backup design

an attacker with CA admin access can extract the CA certificate and private key (built-in backup tools or Mimikatz/SharpDPAPI) and forge authentication certificates for any user. catalog.title: US Reference Collection: Certificate Authority Design and Implementation with Microsoft AD CS (Windows PKI) — Status as of October 2026

spans.t: The US baseline for a Windows enterprise PKI comes from three kinds of source that fit together. Microsoft’s guidance supplies the AD CS–specific design and configuration rules. NIST supplies the cryptographic and key-management rules. CISA/NSA and DISA supply the hardening and detection expectations. The most consistent message across all of them is that
AD CS is Tier 0 identity infrastructure

. Its CA keys, templates and enrollment endpoints can compromise an entire domain, which is why the 2025 Microsoft enforcement changes (strong certificate mapping and NTAuth chaining) are now mandatory with no registry bypass.

blocks.text: 1. TL;DR — summary of the US guidance baseline

spans.t: use a two-tier hierarchy (offline standalone root plus online enterprise issuing CA) for most organizations; avoid single-tier in production; configure CDP/AIA (HTTP-first) before issuing any certificate; renew the CA certificate at half-life; protect CA keys with an HSM where feasible. Since KB5014754 (registry bypass removed September 9, 2025) and KB5057784 (NTAuth bypass support removed October 14, 2025), certificate-based logon fails unless certificates are strongly mapped and chain to a CA in NTAuth. AD CS on Windows Server 2025 gained ML-DSA issuance in May 2026 (KB5087539).

NIST SP 800-57 Pt 1 Rev 5 is still the final key- management reference (Rev 6 was in draft from December 2025). SP 800-131A Rev 2 is the algorithm-transition rule in force (the Rev 3 draft would retire SHA-1/SHA-224 after 2030). The draft NIST IR 8547 proposes deprecating RSA/ECDSA at 112-bit strength after 2030 and disallowing quantum-vulnerable algorithms after 2035. CISA/NSA (jointly with Five Eyes partners) treat AD CS compromise and “Golden Certificate” theft as top-17 AD attack techniques. DISA’s AD Forest STIG makes CA certificate-manager approval and Tier 0 PAW management CAT I (high) requirements.
What is not binding on internal PKI:

the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements, including the 200-day maximum for public TLS since March 15, 2026, falling to 47 days in 2029. Internal AD CS CAs set their own policy. The authorities differ most on validity periods, whether OCSP is required (no US authority mandates it for internal PKI), and how fast to drop RSA/SHA-1. Note also that NIST timelines in late 2026 rest partly on drafts.

design.title: Part V — DHCP in Windows Server and Active Directory: US-Source Design Reference (October 2026)

spans.t: The defensible US-source baseline for enterprise Windows DHCP is: run DHCP on dedicated, AD-authorized member servers (not domain controllers), make it highly available with a two- server DHCP failover relationship, have the DHCP server register DNS records with a dedicated low-privilege credential plus Name Protection rather than via the DnsUpdateProxy group, treat the DHCP Administrators group as a privileged tier, and put the actual anti-rogue/anti-spoofing load on the switch layer (DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, IP Source Guard, RA Guard/DHCPv6-Shield) and on log retention. No US government body publishes a DHCP- specific standard; the IETF RFCs define the protocol, Microsoft defines the Windows implementation, DISA supplies the only hard numeric DHCP rule (log retention), and US practitioner research (Akamai) supplies most of the AD-specific threat analysis.

Deploy Windows DHCP on dedicated domain-member servers authorized in AD (authorization requires Enterprise Admins or delegated rights on the NetServices container); avoid domain controllers, because a DHCP service on a DC inherits DC rights over AD-integrated DNS records and turns “DHCP Administrators” into a path to domain compromise. Use DHCP failover (load balance for co-located partners, hot standby for hub-and-spoke), which current Microsoft Learn documents as requiring Windows Server 2016 or later on both partners; keep split-scope (80/20) only for DHCPv6 or legacy cases.

If the DHCP server must register DNS on clients’ behalf, configure one dedicated, non-privileged DNS-registration credential identical on all DHCP servers, enable Name Protection (DHCID, RFC 4701), keep zones “secure only”, and keep DnsUpdateProxy empty; if DHCP-driven registration is not needed, Akamai’s research recommends disabling it outright.

Message-level DHCP authentication (RFC 3118) is effectively unused, so rogue-server and spoofing protection belongs to the switch and hypervisor (DHCP snooping, DAI, IP Source Guard, Hyper-V DHCP Guard/Router Guard, RA Guard/DHCPv6-Shield); log hostname, MAC, IP and time, and retain DHCP logs 30 days online and 1 year offline — DISA Network Infrastructure Policy STIG V10R7 (2 Aug 2024), rule V-251361 / NET0198 (medium severity), whose fix text reads “Store the logs for a minimum of thirty days online and then offline for one year” — far beyond Windows’ default seven-day rolling audit files.

Microsoft’s failover model is strictly pairwise (a relationship is always between two servers, though one server may hold many relationships), which drives the common pattern of two servers per site or a regional pair plus hub standby. No US authority sets a numeric count; capacity, WAN topology and relay design decide it.

DC co-location saves a server and was historically common in branches, but it couples a broadcast-facing, unauthenticated service to Tier 0 and enlarges the blast radius of DHCP Administrators membership. Dedicated servers cost licences and patching effort but keep DHCP compromise out of Tier 0. AD authorization only governs Windows DHCP servers; a rogue Linux box, router or VM ignores it.

Practice (57% on DCs per Akamai) diverges sharply from current Microsoft and Akamai guidance; Microsoft’s own legacy step-by-step guides used a DC as a DHCP failover partner in examples, while current Microsoft text warns about DC co-location.
How DHCP service survives a server or link failure without duplicate addressing.

(a) DHCP failover, load-balance mode; (b) DHCP failover, hot-standby mode; (c) split-scope (classically 80/20) across two independent servers; (d) Windows Failover Clustering of the DHCP role (shared storage); (e) single standalone server with backup/restore.

Failover “replicates IP address leases and settings” for DHCPv4 scopes from a primary to a partner; both servers hold the whole scope and maintain separate synchronized lease databases — scopes are replicated, not pre-split. Microsoft’s implementation is based on the IETF DHCP Failover Protocol draft (draft- ietf-dhc-failover-12), not on a published RFC; load balancing uses the RFC 3074 MAC-hash bucket mechanism. Partners keep a persistent TCP connection on port 647.

The current Microsoft Learn failover overview (WS2016–WS2025 and Azure Local) states partners “must both be running at least Windows Server 2016.” Legacy Microsoft pages for WS2012/2012 R2 say Windows Server 2012 or later, because the feature was introduced in Windows Server 2012. (Consistent once read as “introduced in 2012; currently documented support floor is 2016.”)

Load balance is the default (50:50, adjustable 0–100%) and “best suited” to partners at the same site; hot standby (default 5% reserve for the standby) suits a central standby backing remote-site servers. Only one mode per relationship/scope; a server may hold relationships in both modes.

The Maximum Client Lead Time is the maximum time one server can extend a lease beyond what its partner knows; a partner that cannot reach its peer renews existing clients only for MCLT and takes over the full pool only after entering PARTNER DOWN and waiting MCLT. The state switchover interval (automatic transition from COMMUNICATION INTERRUPTED to PARTNER DOWN) is optional; without it an administrator must declare partner down manually. Microsoft cmdlet examples use MCLT of 2 hours and a 2-hour auto-switchover.
Optional message authentication between partners; when used with a clustered partner it must be manually replicated to every cluster node.

Changes to failover scopes must be manually replicated (replication overwrites the partner); replicate from the newer-OS partner; clocks must agree within one minute or the wizard halts; both partners must use the same DNS registration credential.

Microsoft retains split-scope as the HA answer for DHCPv6 (failover supports DHCPv4 only) and describes it as viable because DHCPv6 scopes rarely run at high utilization; the 80/20 split-scope wizard dates from Windows Server 2008 R2 SP1-era tooling.
Supported and can be combined with failover (a cluster counts as one failover partner, addressed by cluster name/IP).

Failover gives full-scope availability with lease-state sharing, but adds a replication discipline and a time-sync dependency (cross-reference the NTP design reference). Split-scope needs no inter-server protocol but strands addresses (the 20% server can exhaust) and has no shared lease state. Clustering protects against node failure but not storage or site failure and adds cluster complexity. A long MCLT reduces duplicate-address risk during partitions but delays full-pool takeover; a short one does the reverse.
None between authorities; the main documented “conflict” is the version floor (2012 vs 2016) across Microsoft’s own legacy and current pages.
How subnets map to scopes, which addresses are excluded or reserved, lease duration, option placement, and how to handle multinets and multicast.

, served via relay agents (ip helper) for remote subnets; exclusion ranges for statically addressed infrastructure; reservations (MAC/client-ID bound) for devices needing stable addresses while still receiving centrally managed options.
group multiple scopes for a single physical segment carrying multiple logical subnets (multinet), or during renumbering.
allocate multicast group addresses to MADCAP-aware applications; rarely used in modern enterprises.
Server-level options apply to all scopes; scope options override server options; policy/class-based options override scope options for matching clients; reservation options are most specific and win.

Windows defaults to 8 days for new IPv4 scopes. Shorter leases suit high-churn segments (guest Wi-Fi, conference areas) and shrink stale-record windows but raise renew traffic and dependency on server availability; longer leases suit stable wired desktops and survive longer outages. In failover, renewals during a partition are capped at MCLT regardless of scope lease time.
V- 251362 requires DHCP servers within SIPRNet infrastructure to use a minimum lease duration of 30 days, to support traceability — a classified-network-specific rule, not general guidance.

Many small scopes improve segmentation and Option 82/policy precision but multiply administration; large flat scopes ease management but enlarge broadcast and spoofing domains. Short leases interact with DNS: the dynamic-update page notes DHCP-registered records use a 15-minute TTL by default and that stale A/PTR records require aging/scavenging (cross-reference the DNS design reference).
DISA’s 30-day SIPRNet floor favors attribution; general Microsoft and practitioner guidance favors shorter leases for mobile segments. These are context-dependent, not contradictory.
Which configuration DHCP pushes, at what level, and to which client groups.

003 Router; 006 DNS Servers (internal AD-integrated resolvers for domain clients); 015 DNS Domain Name; 042 NTP Servers (cross-reference the NTP design reference — domain-joined Windows clients normally use the AD domain hierarchy, not option 42); 051 lease time; 066/067 Boot Server Host Name / Bootfile Name for PXE (with modern PXE/WDS/ConfigMgr designs often using IP helpers or policies keyed on vendor class instead of global 066/067); 252 WPAD (proxy auto-discovery; a site-local private- use code, not an IANA standard option); Option 81 client FQDN (RFC 4702) governs DNS registration (§3.5); Option 82 relay agent information (RFC 3046) carries circuit/remote IDs.

DHCP policies (Windows Server 2012 and later) let administrators group clients by vendor class, user class, client identifier, MAC address, relay agent information or FQDN and assign IP ranges and options per group; failover replicates policies with scopes. User classes (client-set, e.g., via
) and vendor classes (e.g., “MSFT 5.0”, PXE client identifiers) remain the classic conditional-delivery mechanisms.

Server-level options minimize duplication but propagate mistakes everywhere; policy-based options give precision at the cost of debugging complexity. Policies keyed on MAC or vendor class are spoofable by the client, so they are configuration conveniences, not security boundaries. Option 252/WPAD and 066/067 are attractive attack targets; Akamai’s escalation research shows that whoever can change options (e.g., the DNS Servers option) can redirect or coerce clients and the server, so option-change rights are security-relevant.
None between authorities; the risk is under-appreciating that option authority equals traffic-steering authority.
Who registers and owns A and PTR records for DHCP clients, with what credential, and how ownership is protected.

(1) Client registers A, server registers PTR (Windows default, Option 81 flag 0). (2) Server always registers A and PTR (“Always dynamically update DNS records”, flag 3), including for non-Windows/legacy clients. (3) Server registers using its machine account (default when no credential configured). (4) Server registers using a dedicated DNS- registration user credential (DHCP > IPv4 > Advanced > Credentials, or

). (5) DnsUpdateProxy membership (records created unsecured so another server or the client can later take ownership). (6) Name Protection (DHCID-based, introduced in Windows Server 2008 R2). (7) Disable DHCP-driven DNS updates entirely.

Members of DnsUpdateProxy register names unsecured, so “the first user to modify the set of records associated with a DNS name becomes its owner”; Microsoft says not to use the group in secure-only AD-integrated zones “without taking additional steps.” It recommends a dedicated standard user account whose credentials multiple DHCP servers can share, and states it must be used when DHCP runs on a DC. It warns that if the credential belongs to a DnsUpdateProxy member, the next registrant becomes owner, and that the DNS credential is not backed up with the DHCP database and must be re-entered after restore. It also advises
, for DHCP-managed Windows clients, because the latter can reset ownership so the DHCP server can no longer update the record.
Both failover partners must use the same DNS credential or updates by the surviving partner fail.

With Name Protection, the server writes a DHCID record and checks it before updating, preventing name squatting by other clients; settings for “discard A and PTR records when lease is deleted” and “dynamically update for clients that do not request updates” sit on the same DNS tab.
Define the DHCID RR and the conflict-resolution procedure that Name Protection implements.

Demonstrated unauthenticated DNS spoofing via DHCP DNS dynamic updates in the default configuration, including overwriting arbitrary records when DHCP runs on a DC (ENTERPRISE DOMAIN CONTROLLERS has write permission on every record in the zone). Microsoft told Akamai a fix is not planned. Mitigations: disable DHCP DNS dynamic updates if not needed; do not use DnsUpdateProxy; use the same weak (non-privileged) DNS credential on all DHCP servers; enable Name Protection (not enabled by default on new scopes); avoid DHCP on DCs. Akamai also notes Name Protection can be partially bypassed (e.g., spoofed DHCP Release) and that the Windows DHCID value is brute-forceable — it raises cost, not certainty.
Treats dynamic-update misuse as a DNS threat, recommends restricting dynamic updates to authorized sources, and recommends correlating DNS query logs with DHCP lease history for incident response.
No DHCP-dynamic- update-specific guidance was located in the reviewed AD-compromise guide text (see Caveats).

DnsUpdateProxy is convenient — any DHCP server or upgraded client can take over records — but leaves records unsecured. A dedicated credential gives clean ownership but becomes a sensitive secret shared across servers and is lost on restore. Server-always-updates gives consistent records for non-Windows devices but means the DHCP server will register names asserted by unauthenticated clients. Disabling DHCP updates removes the attack path but leaves non-Windows devices unregistered.

Older community guidance (widely circulated, including Microsoft-hosted TechNet wiki/forum posts) recommends both DnsUpdateProxy membership and credentials; current Microsoft Learn and Akamai recommend credentials without DnsUpdateProxy.
How to prevent rogue servers, spoofed clients, and privilege escalation through DHCP administration.
DHCP servers; it is not a network control.

DHCP Users have read-only console access; DHCP Administrators can change any DHCP setting, including export/import of configuration and database, but only on the local server and cannot authorize servers. Groups are created at role install (or with
); on a DC they are domain-local groups.

DHCP Administrators can abuse legitimate features (option configuration, DNS Server option plus a coercion scope, relay-agent option) to coerce the DHCP server’s machine account into authenticating to an attacker and relay it (e.g., Kerberos relay to AD CS web enrollment). On a DC this yields domain compromise; the same configuration can serve as stealthy persistence that requires no credentials once set up. Mitigations: treat DHCP Administrators as a high-value group and monitor it; disable DHCP on DCs; harden AD CS against relay (EPA/HTTPS, disable NTLM where possible); block RPC to DHCP servers from non-admin endpoints; block DHCP traffic to/from the internet; watch for DNS anomalies.
Layer-2 controls (NSA Network Infrastructure Security Guide; DISA switch STIGs):

DHCP snooping (trusted uplink ports only; rate-limit on access ports), Dynamic ARP Inspection validated against the snooping binding table, IP Source Guard, port security, and 802.1X/NAC. DISA’s Cisco L2 switch STIG requires DHCP snooping on all user VLANs to validate DHCP messages from untrusted sources. These are switch features, not DHCP-server features.

Hyper-V DHCP Guard drops DHCP server messages from VMs not authorized to act as DHCP servers; Router Guard drops router advertisements and redirects. Both are off by default because of a small performance cost.

RFC 3046 lets relays tag requests with circuit IDs for policy and anti-spoofing; RFC 7513/7039 frame source-address validation that DHCP snooping/IP Source Guard implement; NIST SP 800-189 applies the same source-address-validation principle at inter-domain layer 3.
Useful hygiene, weak security, because MACs are trivially spoofed.

Defined but essentially unimplemented in mainstream clients and servers, including Windows; RFC 9915 retains only Reconfigure-key authentication for DHCPv6. Message authentication is therefore not a practical design control.

CM-6 (configuration settings) and CM- 7 (least functionality — disable unneeded roles such as DHCP on DCs), AC-6 (least privilege for DHCP Administrators), SC-7 (boundary protection — block DHCP/RPC exposure), SI-4 (monitoring).
Network-infrastructure and access-control safeguards (e.g., 12.x secure network infrastructure; 13.9 port-level access control) support snooping/802.1X.

Snooping/DAI/IPSG are the most effective controls but require consistent switch configuration, static-binding exceptions for statically addressed hosts, and trusted-port discipline; misconfiguration causes outages. Tightening DHCP Administrators membership reduces escalation risk but may require new delegation workflows.
None in substance; the gap is that no US authority publishes a Windows-DHCP- server hardening baseline, so the server side is covered by generic host baselines plus vendor research.
Whether hosts get IPv6 addresses via SLAAC, stateless DHCPv6 (options only) or stateful DHCPv6, and how rogue RAs and rogue DHCPv6 servers are blocked.

is the current DHCPv6 base specification, obsoleting RFC 8415; it applies verified errata and obsoletes temporary-address assignment (IA_TA) and the Server Unicast option. DHCPv6 can operate “in place of or in addition to” SLAAC. Router Advertisement M (Managed) and O (Other configuration) flags signal stateful vs stateless DHCPv6 to hosts.
DHCPv6 identifies clients by DUID, not MAC; RFC 6939 lets relays supply the client link-layer address so MAC-based reservations, logging and correlation remain possible.
DHCPv6 has no default-gateway option (gateways come from RAs); DNS servers and search lists are DHCPv6 options; option codes differ from DHCPv4.
Windows DHCP supports stateful and stateless DHCPv6 scopes, but
DHCP failover does not support DHCPv6
; Microsoft recommends identical option configuration on two servers for stateless HA and split-scope for stateful HA. Audit logs for IPv6 are written separately (DhcpV6SrvLog-.log).
RFC 7610 DHCPv6-Shield blocks DHCPv6 server messages on untrusted switch ports; RA Guard blocks rogue RAs; Hyper-V Router Guard drops ICMPv6 type 134 RAs from VMs.

SLAAC is simplest but weakens address-to-host attribution; stateful DHCPv6 improves attribution and DNS registration control but lacks Windows failover. Dual-stack doubles the rogue-server surface: an attacker answering DHCPv6 or sending RAs can capture DNS on IPv4-oriented networks, so IPv6 first-hop controls matter even where IPv6 is “not used.”
None between authorities; the main currency risk is citing RFC 8415 instead of RFC 9915.

Server-side ping before offering (attempts 0–5, default 0), useful when importing scopes or after failures, at a small latency cost.

Time stamps mapped to UTC from an authoritative source — directly relevant because failover also requires partner clocks within one minute; AU-11 audit retention; AU-6 review.

“Use DHCP logging on all DHCP servers or Internet Protocol (IP) address management tools to update the enterprise’s asset inventory,” reviewing logs “weekly, or more frequently”; Control 8 covers collecting, centralizing and retaining audit logs.

Forwarding audit logs to a SIEM satisfies retention and correlation but adds pipeline dependencies; relying on local files violates DISA retention by design. Larger MaxMBFileSize avoids silent pauses but consumes disk. Export-based migration is fast but must be followed by credential re-entry and failover re-establishment.
None; Windows defaults simply fall far short of the DISA requirement.

blocks.text: 4. Where authorities agree, differ, or conflict

spans.t: Agreement: Microsoft positions failover as the default DHCPv4 HA mechanism and split-scope as the DHCPv6/legacy fallback. Difference: Microsoft’s own pages state different version floors (2012 legacy vs 2016 current). No government authority expresses a preference.

Strong agreement among Microsoft’s current dynamic- update guidance and Akamai’s research that DC co-location is risky; Akamai recommends disabling it outright; Microsoft prescribes a dedicated credential if it must occur. Conflict with practice: Akamai observed a DHCP server on a DC in 57% of the networks it saw using Microsoft DHCP. NIST SP 800-81r3 accepts DNS+DHCP co- location, which is a different question.

Microsoft documents the group’s purpose (record takeover across servers/clients) and its risk (unsecured records); Akamai says not to use it. Older community and archived Microsoft-hosted guidance recommending “DnsUpdateProxy plus credentials” conflicts with current guidance.
Context-driven: DISA mandates ≥30 days on SIPRNet for traceability; Microsoft defaults to 8 days; practitioner norms favor hours for guest/wireless. No authority sets a general enterprise value.

Effectively all sources agree it is not: RFC 3118 is defined but unused, Windows does not implement it, and RFC 9915 keeps only Reconfigure-key authentication. Security therefore shifts to layer 2 and to AD authorization.

NIST has no DHCP SP; DISA has no Windows DHCP STIG; CIS has no located DHCP/DnsUpdateProxy benchmark item. The security load is carried by switch controls (NSA guide, DISA switch STIGs), generic controls (SP 800-53, CIS Controls), one DISA logging rule, Microsoft documentation and Akamai research.
Disable DHCP DNS updates vs secure them.

Akamai favors disabling where not required; Microsoft documents secure use (credential plus Name Protection). Both are defensible; the choice depends on whether non-Windows devices need DHCP-registered names.

catalog.title: DHCP for Windows/Enterprise Environments: US-Only Verified Reference Collection (as of October 2026)

spans.t: There is no dedicated US-government DHCP security standard. The US baseline for Windows DHCP is made up of Microsoft’s product documentation, the IETF protocol RFCs, scattered rules in DISA STIGs and one CIS Controls safeguard, with Akamai’s practitioner research filling the security gap. Several items in the prior pass need correcting, notably the failover OS minimum, which mode the reserve percentage belongs to, and the current DHCPv6 RFC.
No US-gov DHCP baseline exists; the guidance is operational, not prescriptive.

NIST has no DHCP Special Publication, CISA/NSA have nothing DHCP-specific, and DISA has no stand-alone DHCP STIG. DHCP shows up only indirectly: in NIST SP 800-81r3 (DNS, March 2026), the DISA Network Infrastructure Policy STIG (DHCP log retention), DISA Layer 2 switch STIGs (DHCP snooping), and CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 1.4 (DHCP logging for asset inventory). Microsoft Learn and the IETF RFCs are therefore the primary technical sources.
Microsoft’s operational model is confirmed, with corrections.
Microsoft calls DHCP Failover “the preferred option,” with two modes: load balance (the default, 50:50) and hot standby. The default 5% reserve percentage belongs to
, not load balance. The shared secret is optional. The current Learn page requires both partners to run
(the feature first shipped in Server 2012). Microsoft also confirms the BPA statement “Name protection requires secure update to work. Without name protection DNS names may be hijacked.”
The main security risk is in DHCP-to-DNS integration, and the vendor won’t patch it.

Akamai (US company; non-governmental research) found that DHCP DNS Dynamic Updates “don’t require any credentials, and work with the default configuration” and that Microsoft does not plan a fix. A follow-on post showed DHCP Administrators can reach domain admin when DHCP runs on a domain controller. Logging is the one control that every source agrees on.

spans.t: Every federal source treats DHCP indirectly: as a DNS client (NIST), a log source (DISA, CIS), or a switch-layer threat (DISA L2S). Microsoft’s product documentation is effectively the configuration baseline.
DDNS is unauthenticated by design, and Microsoft won’t patch it.

Microsoft’s documentation frames the risk as record ownership. Akamai shows unauthenticated overwrite under default settings and reports that no fix is planned. NIST’s “authorized senders only” principle is satisfied only at the DHCP→DNS hop, not client→DHCP. That gap is the core conflict.
DHCP on a DC vs. tiering.
Microsoft documents that DC-hosted DHCP “inherits the security permissions of the domain controller” but does not forbid it.
DISA’s legacy V-4501 and both Akamai posts argue against it.
NIST 800-81r3 allows co-locating DHCP with DNS when dedicated servers aren’t feasible. That speaks to DNS servers, not DCs, so it is not a direct contradiction.
keep DHCP off DCs. If you can’t, set a dedicated low-privilege DNS credential.
Rogue defense is layered, and no single source covers it all.
AD authorization (Microsoft) stops only Windows servers.
DHCP snooping (DISA L2S) and RFC 7610 / RA Guard cover IPv4/IPv6 at layer 2.
There is no usable DHCP protocol authentication.
RFC 3118 is effectively unused, and DHCPv6 delayed authentication was obsoleted in RFC 8415. The only “authentication” in Windows DHCP is the optional failover shared secret.
Logging is the one clean agreement.

spans.t: DISA’s Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIGs) are the DoD’s product-specific configuration standards, derived from DISA Security Requirements Guides (SRGs) that are in turn derived from NIST SP 800-53 via Control Correlation Identifiers (CCIs); the current quarterly DISA GPO package is “Group Policy Objects (GPOs) - October 2026,” uploaded to the DoD Cyber Exchange on 2026-10-16, and the current STIG Viewer is 3.8.1 (released October 2, 2026).

STIGs (XCCDF-formatted, rule-by-rule hardening requirements rated CAT I/II/III) and SRGs (technology-class requirements that “are derived from the NIST 800-53 and related documents”) are published by the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) on the DoD Cyber Exchange (cyber.mil, formerly public.cyber.mil). DoDI 8510.01 (RMF for DoD; 2014 text, RMF Step 3) requires that products in a system boundary “be configured in accordance with applicable STIGs or SRGs where STIGs are not available.” The DISA GPO package (latest: October 2026, uploaded 2026-10-16) is an implementation aid containing ADMX templates, GPO backup exports, GPO reports, WMI filter exports and STIG checklist files that cover “most applicable GPO STIG settings”. It is not the STIG itself.

each STIG rule cites one or more CCIs, and each CCI decomposes an SP 800-53 control into a single, actionable statement. NIST’s National Checklist Program (NCP) re-lists DISA STIGs (with SCAP 1.4 content and links to the DISA GPO package) alongside CIS and vendor checklists. Assessment is done with DISA STIG Viewer 3.8.1 (CKL/CKLB checklists), the Navy’s SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC 5.15, NIWC Atlantic, released 09/01/2026), and optionally the Navy’s Evaluate-STIG (NSWC Crane/NAVSEA) and STIG Manager (NUWC Newport, open source).

unclassified STIGs, SRGs, SCAP benchmarks, the GPO package, STIG Viewer and SCC are free, public downloads from cyber.mil. CAC/PKI is needed only for restricted content and some tools’ distribution points (e.g., Evaluate-STIG on NAVSEA’s SPORK). The comparison baselines are CIS Benchmarks (consensus-based, free PDF under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, with a STIG profile that replaced the former Level 3) and Microsoft security baselines in the Security Compliance Toolkit (SCT 1.0, Download Center page dated 10/8/2026). The Windows STIGs build on the Microsoft baselines and generally exceed them.

CCI “provides a standard identifier and description for each of the singular, actionable statements that comprise an IA control or IA best practice,” bridging “high-level policy expressions and low-level technical implementations.”

STIG and SRG rules cite CCIs (e.g., CCI-001453 maps to AC-17); CCIs map to SP 800- 53 controls (current Rev 5 CCIs include IDs in the CCI-004xxx range). DoDI 8510.01 tasks DISA to ensure CCIs, SRGs and STIGs are consistent with DoD security controls and assessment procedures.
DISA’s CCI process document (draft V1R0.1) states DISA established the initial CCI List from SP 800-53 and accepts proposed changes by email (cci@disa.mil).
Where to get the list (conflicting sources):

one DAU Acquipedia version says that “As of 2021, the CCI List is no longer published on the DOD Cyber Exchange” and directs users to export CCIs from STIGs via STIG Viewer; another version says the CCI list “has moved to the STIG Document Library downloads section.” STIG Viewer 3.7 release notes cite an “Updated CCI List” bundled in the tool. Treat STIG Viewer and the STIG Document Library as the current routes.

DISA’s legacy download page describes two tiers: “DoD Cyber Exchange Public (public.cyber.mil),” with “limited access to publicly releasable cyber training and guidance to all Internet users,” and “DoD Cyber Exchange NIPR (cyber.mil),” with exclusive access for DoD PKI credential holders. Current www.cyber.mil pages carry the banner “Login with DoD CAC for full access.”

Unclassified STIGs, SRGs, SCAP benchmarks, the GPO and Intune packages, STIG Viewer and SCC are listed as “Unclassified” and are publicly downloadable. Some STIGs and supporting content (and Evaluate-STIG) require DoD PKI.

Recent DISA documents use “Department of War (DoW)” wording in places alongside “DOD”; cyber.mil content is being migrated, and some legacy pages (e.g., Cyber Workforce content) are slated to sunset December 31, 2026.

blocks.text: 4. Section B — Related US government and standards guidance

spans.t: SP 800-53 Rev 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

— NIST; Sept 2020 (updated Dec 2020); current; free, US government work (public domain in the US). Scope: the control catalog the SRGs/STIGs implement via CCIs. Key point: controls are outcome-oriented, not product settings; STIGs supply the product-level settings for configuration controls such as CM-6 (configuration settings) and CM-7 (least functionality).

— https://ncp.nist.gov (also reachable via nvd.nist.gov/ncp/repository); current; free. Scope: centralized repository of security configuration checklists from authoritative sources. Key points: lists DISA STIGs with authority “Governmental Authority: Defense Information Systems Agency,” review status, type (Compliance), and links to SCAP content, standalone XCCDF, GPO and Intune packages — e.g., Windows 10 STIG V3R7 (Checklist ID 629) links “Group Policy Objects (GPOs) - July 2026” and SCAP 1.4 content. NCP also hosts CIS Benchmarks, which carry CIS’s CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licence text.
SP 800-70, National Checklist Program for IT Products: Guidelines for Checklist Users and Developers
— NIST. The Rev 5 IPD was released Dec 9, 2025, with comments due Jan 16, 2026. NIST CSRC lists Rev 5 as final on May 8, 2026 (authors

Stephen Quinn and Blair Heiserman, DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-70r5), superseding Rev 4 (02/15/2018). Rev 5 adds mappings between checklist settings, CSF 2.0 outcomes, SP 800-53 controls and CCE identifiers.

the Tier I–IV scheme (Tier I prose- based through Tier IV complete SCAP-validated content) is from Rev 3; Rev 4 “Removed the checklist ‘tier’ and ‘SCAP Expressed’ concepts,” so NCP listings now describe automation by content type (prose vs SCAP) rather than tier. The NCP participant page still listed Rev 5 as an initial public draft at time of research.

Key points: SCAP 1.4 “is the current final release”; Rev 4 removes backward-compatibility requirements for earlier SCAP versions, revises digital-signature requirements, and redirects OVAL references to the OVAL Community GitHub. NIST credits NIWC Atlantic’s team (Jack Vander Pol is a co-author) with shaping the revision. SCAP 1.3 (Rev 3) is superseded; NIST’s SCAP Content Validation Tool supports 1.2, 1.3 and 1.4.

— DoD CIO; effective July 19, 2022 (reissued and cancelled the March 12, 2014 “RMF for DoD IT” version); current; public. blocks.text: 6. Where authorities agree, differ, or conflict

spans.t: both target secure configuration and overlap heavily on Windows/Linux settings. The difference is authority and process: STIGs are DoD- mandated and DISA-approved (often vendor-authored); CIS Benchmarks are consensus products. CIS’s STIG profile explicitly bridges the two and flags contradictions with CIS recommendations — the clearest sign the baselines are not identical. CIS STIG
Benchmark versions (e.g., Windows Server 2022 STIG 3.0.0) track specific DISA releases and can lag DISA’s quarterly updates.
STIG GPO package vs Microsoft baseline:

both are delivered as GPO backups with reports and WMI filters, and DISA’s Windows GPOs largely start from the same Windows settings. DISA adds DoD-specific and stricter values and omits settings that need organizational values (placeholders); Microsoft ships LGPO and Policy Analyzer, while DISA’s package (per available evidence) does not bundle LGPO. Use Policy Analyzer to see exact deltas for a given release pair.

CAT I–III rates DoD impact of a weakness; CVSS scores software vulnerabilities (CVEs); CIS Level 1/2/STIG are profile scopes; CIS Implementation Groups (IG1–IG3) belong to the CIS Controls, not the Benchmarks. A CAT I finding is not equivalent to a “critical” CVSS score.

DISA is quarterly (2026 releases arrived early in Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct months, e.g., Oct 6), with GPOs a few weeks later (Oct 16); Microsoft ships per OS/app release (e.g., Windows 11 26H2 baseline in September 2026, ahead of a DISA STIG for that build); CIS targets 90 days after a Windows release. Expect periods when the newest Windows build has a Microsoft baseline but not yet a matching STIG update.
SCAP benchmarks (SCC) automate only part of a STIG; the remainder is manual (STIG Viewer) or semi-automated (Evaluate-STIG). A clean SCC score is not full STIG compliance.

STIGs are required for DoD systems per DoDI 8510.01, but are freely usable elsewhere as hardening references; NIST NCP lists them for broad use. Non-DoD frameworks (e.g., NIST SP 800-171/CMMC) do not name STIGs as the required baseline (per secondary sources).

the Quarterly Release Schedule page’s Q4 row still reads “End of October 2025”; Windows Server 2025 versioning differs between the October announcement (STIG V1R4) and the SCAP benchmark (V1R2, uploaded 2026-10- 05) — SCAP benchmark release numbers are tracked separately from STIG release numbers, so always match the benchmark to the STIG release named in its readme.

spans.t: cyber.mil pages render via JavaScript and could not be fetched in full; DISA facts were verified from indexed page text of cyber.mil, DISA PDFs (dl.dod.cyber.mil), and NIST NCP listings.

The Windows Server 2025 STIG release is reported as V1R4 (October 6 announcement snippet) by one source and V1R2 by trackers; the SCAP benchmark is V1R2. Confirm on the STIG Document Library.
Evaluate-STIG’s current version is behind CAC; not verified. STIG Manager’s and SCC’s licence terms were not reviewed in detail.
One third-party source claims SCC downloads are CAC-gated; NIWC Atlantic states SCC has been publicly available from DISA since 5.4 — the primary source is preferred.
CCI list publication location is described inconsistently by DAU sources; the date of DISA’s V-/SV- renumbering was not re-verified.

SP 800-70 Rev 5 is listed as final on NIST CSRC (May 8, 2026, superseding Rev 4 of 02/15/2018), but the NCP participant page still shows the draft. SP 800-37 Rev 2 (final 12/20/2018) and SP 800-137 (final 09/30/2011) dates are confirmed on CSRC. SP 800-53 Rev 5 minor releases, SP 800-117 and CNSSI 1253 versions were not re-verified in this session.

DoDI 8500.01’s configuration and DISA-tasking wording was confirmed from the quotation in NIST NCP’s DISA checklist entry rather than from the instruction itself. DoDI 8510.01’s STIG/SRG language (“configured in accordance with applicable STIGs or SRGs where STIGs are not available”) was confirmed from the 2014 text, and the 2022 reissue’s existence and effective date were confirmed separately.
Third-party trackers (stigviewer.com, cyber.trackr.live, stigaview.com) were used only for rule counts and SRG versions and are not authoritative.

US government works (DISA, NIST, NSA, DoD) are generally not subject to US copyright, but vendor-co-developed STIGs and bundled third-party files may carry other terms; DISA does not publish a single explicit reuse licence that was verified here.
